entries.name: day-trader-skill (Jakeschincariol)
entries.what_it_does: A pack of 11 Claude Skills for day trading — not an autonomous bot. Each skill is a SKILL.md plus a small stdlib-only Python tool: a scanner (~5,900 US stocks, opening-range breakouts etc.), news, entry timer, exit planner, a 'Time Machine' (10,000 Monte-Carlo replays of a trade), risk, budget/position-sizing, broker, alerts, an earnings analyst, and a Congress-trades tracker. Skills chain via a shared folder, read free public data (Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq Trader, SEC EDGAR), need no API key, default to paper trading, and no order goes through without an explicit human yes after the risk check.
entries.fit_rationale: The skill-pack structure (scanner → risk → budget chain with a human-yes gate) mirrors Stratex's governed pipeline and is worth mining for the RD programme's workflow design. The strategies themselves are US-equities day-trading content — they enter only through the same RD evidence bar as everything else, demo-only. Single-commit repo: copy patterns, don't depend on it.

entries.name: claude-trading-skills (tradermonty)
entries.what_it_does: A Claude Skills workflow toolkit for individual equity investors: 74 skills across market regime/breadth, portfolio, dividend income, swing screeners (CANSLIM, VCP, FinViz), trade planning, trade memory/journaling and strategy research, plus workflow manifests and pre-built packages for Claude Web. It structures review, risk management, planning and post-mortems; it is explicitly not a signal service and does not place orders. A starter path runs on free public CSVs with no API key; some screeners optionally use paid data (FMP, FinViz Elite, Alpaca).
entries.fit_rationale: The trade-memory/journaling and structured review/post-mortem skills are the valuable part for Stratex's forward-test discipline. Actively maintained and MIT. Paid-data screeners stay out (free tiers only).

entries.name: claude-trading-skills (agiprolabs)
entries.what_it_does: A different repo with the same name: 68 trading, DeFi and quantitative-finance Agent Skills in the open Agent Skills format, working with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI and 30+ other tools. Crypto/DeFi-first: market-data APIs (Birdeye, DexScreener, CoinGecko, Helius, DeFiLlama), Solana infrastructure, on-chain/whale analysis, technical analysis, backtesting (vectorbt/Backtrader, walk-forward), portfolio/risk (incl. Kelly criterion), DeFi/LP/yield, statistics, ML for trading, execution, microstructure, options pricing, prediction markets and tax/compliance. Analysis/research only.
entries.language: Markdown SKILL.md files with Python examples
entries.fit_rationale: A broad pattern catalogue — cherry-pick backtesting and risk skill patterns for the RD programme rather than adopting wholesale. Crypto/DeFi emphasis overlaps Stratex's venues, but the repo is thinly maintained.

entries.name: OpenBB (Open Data Platform)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source financial data platform: integrate proprietary, licensed and public data sources once and consume them everywhere — a Python SDK (pip install openbb), the OpenBB Workspace/Excel for analysts, MCP servers for AI agents, and REST APIs. Covers equities, crypto, derivatives, economics, fixed income and options. (The repo now renders under openbq-org stewardship; v5, Sep 2026, relicensed from AGPL-3.0 to Apache-2.0 — earlier releases remain AGPL.)
entries.fit_rationale: The natural data backbone candidate for Futuris forecasting inputs (and the openbb_routes Stratex already carries). The full platform is far too heavy for the current ~1GB servers — adopt selectively (Python SDK / MCP surface) and only post-ARM. Apache-2.0 removes the old AGPL concern for new versions.

entries.name: OpenTerminal (ErTasselli)
entries.what_it_does: A terminal-style, self-hosted trading dashboard built entirely on free public market data — no API keys, no subscriptions. Dark, dense, keyboard-driven widget workspace (drag/resize, persisted layouts): professional charting (candlesticks, 8 timeframes, SMA/EMA/VWAP/Bollinger/RSI/MACD), quotes, watchlists, a full-market screener, live sector heatmap, options chain, crypto board, macro dashboard, portfolio tracker (SQLite), economic/earnings calendar, aggregated news, a command palette, and an optional Claude assistant. Data is stitched from free endpoints (Nasdaq, TradingView, Yahoo/Stooq, CoinGecko/Binance, FRED) with fallback chains.
entries.fit_rationale: Its dense multi-panel composition is already stored as the 'trading-terminal' design candidate. The TypeScript stack doesn't fit the fleet's Python services; the transferable assets are the layout and the free-data fallback-chain pattern.

entries.name: NautilusTrader
entries.what_it_does: A production-grade, Rust-native algorithmic trading engine with a deterministic event-driven architecture spanning research, backtesting and live execution in one system — the same strategy code runs in backtest and live with no reimplementation. Python is the control plane (Rust-only also possible). Asset-class-agnostic with modular adapters for crypto CEX/DEX, FX, equities, futures, options and brokers (Binance, Bybit, Coinbase, Kraken, OKX, Hyperliquid, Interactive Brokers, Polymarket, Kalshi), and nanosecond-resolution historical tick/bar/order-book backtesting.
entries.fit_rationale: The backtest=live parity discipline is the design lesson for Stratex's rig. As a runtime it is far beyond the ~1GB servers and unnecessary for the current demo venues (Binance demo-fapi, OANDA practice) — do not adopt; revisit only if the fleet gets real hardware.

entries.name: Hermes Agent (Nous Research)
entries.what_it_does: A self-improving, self-hosted personal AI agent: a built-in learning loop creates skills from experience and improves them in use; agent-curated persistent memory with cross-session recall and full-text search; it builds a model of the user. Runs anywhere (laptop, small VPS, GPU cluster, serverless), works with any model provider, and is reachable via a terminal TUI and a single messaging gateway (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, CLI), with cron scheduling, sub-agent delegation and MCP integration. Several corpus tools (Herald OS, AgentOS, MausBot) build on or alongside it.
entries.fit_rationale: FRIDAY Universe already implements this pattern (10-agent fleet + Memora), so adopting it would mean replacing FRIDAY. The transferable assets are its skill-learning loop and memory design — mine those for Memora/FRIDAY, don't adopt the platform.

entries.name: Herald OS
entries.what_it_does: An agent-native operating-system layer with Hermes Agent as the interface (independent project, not affiliated with Nous Research; Hermes is installed alongside, not forked). Instead of menus and folders you talk/type to the agent to open apps, find and organise files, watch what is running, remember what matters, run scheduled routines and build software — with every state-changing action going through a permission system the user controls. Ships as a Fedora-based Linux OS and a fullscreen macOS app. Status: alpha (0.1).
entries.fit_rationale: Alpha software — do not adopt. Its permission-gated mission UX and morning-briefing flow are the takeaway, and FRIDAY already has both behaviours; compare details during the voice/UX work.

entries.name: OpenClaw
entries.what_it_does: An open-source personal AI assistant that runs on your own computer and meets you in the channels you already use (Discord, iMessage, Slack, Teams, Telegram, WhatsApp and 20+ more), with native apps for macOS, iOS, Android, Windows and Linux. A single local Gateway is the control plane for sessions, tools, events and channel connections. State, memory and credentials live on your hardware; models and agent harnesses (Claude, Codex, local models) are swappable plugins. Stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation; no paid tier or hosted service.
entries.fit_rationale: A competing personal-assistant platform — adopting it would replace FRIDAY. The channel-gateway control-plane pattern is the lesson (FRIDAY's bridge/mesh plays this role today).

entries.name: MausBot (OpenMausBot)
entries.what_it_does: A free, open-source desktop app (Electron/React) that unifies existing agent CLIs in one Telegram-style chat UI: every sidebar contact is a real bot — Claude Code, Codex, Grok and other engines (16 claimed, incl. Hermes and OpenClaw) running locally on the plan/API key you already have — each with its own personality, model, memory and connected apps. Data lives locally; bots can surface approval cards before acting. (An enterprise/ folder is source-available under a separate licence.)
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (enterprise/ folder under a separate source-available licence)
entries.fit_rationale: The unified multi-agent shell UX is the reference for Forge's builder-environment idea. A heavyweight Electron desktop app — not a fit for the 1GB servers, and FRIDAY's fleet already has its own coordination surface.

entries.name: JCode
entries.what_it_does: A high-performance coding-agent harness written in Rust, built for heavy multi-agent/multi-session work. Its pitch is extreme efficiency vs Claude Code / Codex CLI — its README benchmarks claim ~71MB for the first headless session and ~3.3MB per additional session (vs ~169MB / ~194MB) and ~19ms time-to-first-input. It includes automatic semantic memory (each turn embedded and queried against a memory graph), parallel sessions coordinated by a server, a swarm tool where agents spawn/message collaborators and resolve file conflicts, built-in browser automation, many providers including Claude/Codex OAuth, and a self-dev mode.
entries.fit_rationale: The most hardware-honest tool in the corpus: its tiny footprint is exactly the shape FRIDAY's ~1GB servers demand. Evaluate as a reference architecture — and possibly a pilot harness — for Forge's build runtime (lean prompt/memory/session layer, parallel sessions, lead + helper agents).

entries.name: Project NOMAD (Crosstalk Solutions)
entries.what_it_does: A self-contained, offline-first knowledge and education server ('Node for Offline Media, Archives, and Data'). A Docker-orchestrated management UI/API installs and manages containerised tools for use with no internet after initial setup: offline Wikipedia/medical references/ebooks via Kiwix, Khan Academy via Kolibri, downloadable offline maps via ProtoMaps, local AI chat with document upload and RAG via Ollama + Qdrant, CyberChef, FlatNotes, and a one-click app catalogue. Zero built-in telemetry; by design it has no authentication and is not meant to be exposed directly to the internet.
entries.fit_rationale: The pattern source for FRIDAY's offline-first fallback mode (local LLM + local knowledge store). The full Docker stack is too heavy for the current servers — adopt the pattern in miniature now, fuller version post-ARM (Qdrant is already in FRIDAY's post-ARM plan).

entries.name: AURA (aura-android-use)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source Android app that puts an MCP server inside the phone. An on-device agent reads the screen via the accessibility tree plus on-device vision (YOLOv8/OCR), then taps/types/scrolls in real apps — no root, no cable, no relay server. The same 45–50+ tools are exposed over MCP so Claude Code / Cursor / any MCP client on a computer can drive the phone; computer and phone must share a Wi-Fi network (LAN-only encrypted WebRTC bridge, PIN pairing). Bring-your-own key from 13 providers; includes voice input and a hard safety gate that blocks banking/payment/authenticator apps and secret entry. Solo-built and self-described as unstable. (Name collision: the unrelated voice-assistant 'AURA' in video Da6PwA8z-wq is a different thing.)
entries.fit_rationale: A possible shortcut for exactly what PHONE-001 lacks today (tap/swipe/screenshot — the Termux executor can't). But: AGPL + commercial dual licensing, one maintainer, unstable. Pilot carefully on the owner's phone; do not build production dependence on it. Google's ARTEMIS (below) is the safer primary candidate.

entries.name: ARTEMIS (Google)
entries.what_it_does: Google's open-source framework that turns natural-language instructions into reliable automation on a real Android phone or emulator (via USB debugging/ADB). It observes screenshot + UI hierarchy + OCR, acts via ADB/UIAutomator2, and captures Logcat/screenshots. Four interfaces: web console, CLI, Python SDK, and a native MCP server (5 tools) that plugs into Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor and others. Two execution profiles: Flash (reactive loop, ~3–5s/step) and Pro (planner/operator/checker). Google Research claims 99%+ on its AndroidWorld benchmark (self-reported).
entries.fit_rationale: The strongest candidate to give FRIDAY's phone control real UI automation (see screen → tap/type through real apps) beyond PHONE-001's Termux executor. Apache-2.0 and Google-maintained. Caveats: Python 3.12+ (fleet production is 3.10 — run it laptop-side, not on the servers) and it needs an ADB path to the phone, which is an owner-side setup step.

entries.name: scrcpy (Genymobile)
entries.what_it_does: Mirrors an Android device (video + audio) to Linux/Windows/macOS over USB or TCP/IP and lets you control it with the computer's keyboard and mouse. No root, nothing left installed on the device, no account or internet required. Focused on lightness and performance (30–120 fps, 35–70ms latency, ~1s startup); features include audio forwarding, recording, virtual display, screen-off mirroring, bidirectional copy-paste, camera mirroring and HID input.
entries.fit_rationale: The proven transport for Android screen mirror + control that PHONE-001's Termux executor lacks. Mature, tiny, Apache-2.0 — adopt as the mirror/control layer alongside the existing phone bridge.

entries.name: Browser Use
entries.what_it_does: An open-source browser-agent library: give it a task and the model does it in a real browser, writing Python in one persistent REPL against raw Chrome DevTools Protocol with browser-harness helpers. Runs on any LLM, locally (local Chromium / your own Chrome profile) or via the separate paid Browser Use Cloud (stealth browsers, CAPTCHA solving, hosted Agents API). v1.0 rewrite shipped Nov 2026; the README warns to pin the version exactly.
entries.fit_rationale: The concrete implementation behind the corpus's browser-use idea (FRIDAY agents operating a real browser). MIT and Python — but it needs Python 3.11+ while production runs 3.10 (the REL-050 constraint), so run it laptop-side or after the fleet Python upgrade. Skip the paid cloud.

entries.name: net-merge
entries.what_it_does: A free tool to use all your internet connections at once on Windows, macOS, Linux and Android. It creates a virtual TUN adapter and load-balances new connections across Wi-Fi, Ethernet, mobile data and phone tethers — no account, no server, no VPN. Its own README states the key limit honestly: a single connection stays on a single link, so one single-stream download does not get faster; gains come from apps that open many connections (Steam, browsers, torrents, download managers).
entries.fit_rationale: A handy owner-side utility with no FRIDAY-agent role. If Surendra wants faster downloads on his own machines it works as-is; nothing to implement into the fleet.

entries.name: Plexo
entries.what_it_does: A free, open-source desktop download manager (Windows/macOS/Linux, Electron) that speeds up a single download: it splits one file into chunks via HTTP range requests and downloads chunks in parallel across every selected connection (Wi-Fi + Ethernet + USB-tethered phone), balancing load, racing slow tail chunks, then reassembling and verifying the file. Also handles torrents, magnet/.torrent and Usenet NZBs, browser-extension capture, pause/resume and scheduling. Caveat from its README: each network needs its own upstream — Wi-Fi + Ethernet on the same router adds nothing. Pre-release (v1.0.0-rc), installers not yet code-signed.
entries.fit_rationale: Owner-side utility, no FRIDAY-agent role. Unlike net-merge it genuinely accelerates single downloads; usable by the owner as-is once it hits 1.0.

entries.name: Paperclip
entries.what_it_does: An open-source orchestration platform for teams of AI agents — 'If OpenClaw is an employee, Paperclip is the company.' A self-hosted Node.js server + React UI that hires agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenClaw, etc.) into an org chart (CEO/CTO/engineers/marketers) with goals, tasks/tickets, heartbeats, per-agent budgets, approvals/governance and audit logs. Bring-your-own-agent; no account required.
entries.fit_rationale: Its org-chart + budgets + approvals governance mirrors FRIDAY's board/coordination model — mine the governance patterns. Running another Node orchestration server alongside the fleet on ~1GB VMs is not viable.

entries.name: claude-mem
entries.what_it_does: Persistent memory for coding agents. A second 'observer' agent records everything a coding agent does in a session, compresses it with AI, and injects a compact index of relevant context into future sessions so the agent doesn't restart from zero. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Hermes, Copilot and more; memory is stored locally (~/.claude-mem), cloud sync opt-in.
entries.fit_rationale: The observer-agent session-compression pattern is a concrete design input for Memora (how coding/build sessions should be remembered). Built for coding-agent CLIs, so adapt the pattern rather than dropping it in.

entries.name: Agent Reach
entries.what_it_does: A free, read-only CLI 'capability layer' that gives an AI agent eyes on the internet: it installs/tests the best upstream tool per platform (yt-dlp, gh, Jina Reader, bili-cli, etc.) and exposes 14 channels behind one command — YouTube, GitHub, web/RSS and V2EX/Bilibili with no login; X/Twitter, Reddit, LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, Xiaohongshu and others via a dedicated background browser / copied login. It only fetches — no posting, comments, likes or DMs.
entries.fit_rationale: A direct fit for IntelX's social-link reader idea, and its Python 3.10+ requirement matches production's interpreter (rare in this corpus). Read-only by design, which suits IntelX's research remit. Care: the logged-in channels use the owner's accounts via a background browser — use no-login channels by default.

entries.name: FreeLLM API (FreeLLMAPI)
entries.what_it_does: A self-hosted, OpenAI-compatible (plus Anthropic/Gemini/Ollama surfaces) router that pools the free tiers of many providers behind one local endpoint and one unified key. Its README headline claims 87 free providers, 1,313 free model endpoints and ~10.1B tokens/month aggregate, with smart routing, automatic failover on rate limits, per-key usage tracking, encrypted key storage, an admin dashboard and desktop apps. Stated as 'personal experimentation only'; free installs receive the model catalogue 30 days behind the paid live feed.
entries.fit_rationale: Inference already implements this exact pattern in production (multi-provider key pool, failover, quota ledger, best-suitable routing) — the corpus's own classification marks the idea already-implemented. Do not duplicate it; the only cherry-pick is comparing catalogue breadth.

entries.name: OmniRoute
entries.what_it_does: A free, self-hosted AI gateway for coding tools (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Cline, Copilot, OpenCode). One local endpoint routes across 375+ providers (150+ free; 1,400+ models) using 'combos' — quota-aware fallback chains ordered Subscription → API → Cheap → Free — plus token compression (claimed 15–95% savings), MCP/A2A support and a dashboard. Its ~1.62B free-tokens/month headline is explicitly an aggregate of third-party free tiers you connect yourself, not a grant. (Original address diegosouzapw/OmniRoute redirects here.)
entries.fit_rationale: Same pattern as Inference's production gateway (which the corpus marks already-implemented for this idea family). The cherry-pick is its token-compression idea for squeezing free-tier quotas; do not adopt the gateway itself.

entries.name: Strata
entries.what_it_does: A local MoE inference engine that runs very large models on consumer hardware by treating experts as a cache: hot experts stay in GPU VRAM, the rest tier across system RAM and SSD. Ships desktop and terminal apps, serves OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs on localhost for Claude Code/Codex/OpenCode, no account or telemetry. Launch models include a 125B-class Qwen MoE and DeepSeek Flash; reference hardware is a 12GB consumer GPU + ~64GB RAM. IMPORTANT CORRECTION: the reel frames Strata as a way to run a 125B model on free Kaggle GPUs — the repo does not support that framing; it targets your own consumer PC (Cloudflare Tunnel is only an optional remote-access mode). The Kaggle dual-T4 guides that exist are for other projects.
entries.fit_rationale: Reject for the fleet: it needs a 12GB GPU and ~64GB RAM; the Oracle servers have neither, and there is no Kaggle path in the repo despite the video's claim. At most a future experiment on the owner's own PC.

entries.name: needle / Cactus (cactus-compute)
entries.what_it_does: Cactus Compute's tiny on-device foundation-model family, built only for tool/function calling, structured extraction and embeddings — not chat. Needle 2 is a 45M-parameter model shipped as a single 14MB binary that runs a full session in ~28MB RAM, fully offline on phones, wearables, Raspberry Pi and microcontrollers, emitting structured JSON tool calls with a confidence score. The canonical repo is now the unified 'cactus' Python package (pip install cactus-compute) bundling Needle (agents), Whistle (speech-to-text) and Mirage (vision) on their native engine; the old cactus-compute/needle repo is a redirect stub.
entries.language: Python package over a native C++ engine
entries.fit_rationale: A genuine fit for the corpus's tiny-on-device-model idea: an always-available, offline fast path for simple FRIDAY commands on the owner's phone/laptop (28MB RAM is nothing). Pilot on-device; the servers don't need it.

entries.name: PentAGI
entries.what_it_does: A self-hosted, fully autonomous multi-agent penetration-testing platform. Specialised agents (researcher, planner, executor, advisers/reflectors/memorists) research a target, plan the test, and run 20+ real security tools (Nmap, SQLMap, Metasploit, etc.) inside isolated Docker sandboxes, storing findings in PostgreSQL/pgvector with an optional knowledge graph, then produce a report. Supports cloud LLMs or local models via Ollama/vLLM. Its docs stress authorised targets only (separate EULA).
entries.fit_rationale: Far too heavy for the fleet (Docker sandboxes + Postgres + Neo4j on ~1GB VMs) and offensive in remit, while Sentinel is defensive. Mine the specialised-agent role design only; any real use would need separate hardware and the owner's explicit authorisation.

entries.name: Uplika (uplika-mcp setup repo)
entries.what_it_does: Uplika is a hosted MCP server that lets an AI agent (Claude, Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT) publish text/images/video to connected social accounts (Threads, Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, TikTok, Pinterest, Bluesky, Telegram, Discord, Ghost), schedule posts, read/reply to comments, hide comments, and read insights/analytics — the corpus video uses it to run a YouTube channel (analytics → winning formats → titles/hooks/descriptions → scheduling → comments) behind human approval. CRITICAL CAVEAT from its own README: this repository holds setup notes only — 'The server itself is a hosted service and its code is not published here.' The repo is a single README (3 commits, ~2 stars). The service is commercial: free plan/beta, then $10/mo per brand per its terms.
entries.license: Not stated (no LICENSE in repo; server closed-source)
entries.language: None — no code in the repo
entries.fit_rationale: Adopt the pattern, not the dependency: the approval-gated channel-operator loop is exactly VyralX's agent-operated-channel idea, and VyralX should implement it natively (it also sidesteps VyralX's dead YouTube OAuth only if Uplika's own YouTube connection works — unproven). The hosted service itself is recurring paid spend ($10/mo/brand), which stays the owner's call.

entries.name: Hypit
entries.what_it_does: A system that gives AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, etc.) a language (its SVML markup) to create video. You drop in a reference video and the agent clones it as a complete, editable, re-runnable workflow — footage, word-level captions, B-roll and effects, all anchored to words instead of seconds — so you can swap the host, topic, hook, language or aspect ratio and render many variants ('1 command, 100 variants'). It installs as an agent Skill; generation models are optional/pluggable (own API keys, local models, or its paid HypiHub service), so code-rendered clones can cost $0 while AI-generated footage costs money (~$1.07–1.15 per example clone in its README).
entries.license: Custom 'Hypit Open Source License' (GitHub: Other/NOASSERTION) — free inside your own organisation; hosting as a multi-tenant service or reselling requires a commercial licence; outputs belong to the user
entries.fit_rationale: The concrete engine behind VyralX's viral-format cloning idea (its #1 content-pattern idea). The licence permits internal use, which is exactly VyralX's case. Keep renders code-based/$0 or on free tiers; per-clone AI-footage costs are spend to avoid by default.

entries.name: HyperFrames (HeyGen)
entries.what_it_does: HeyGen's free, open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media and seekable animations (GSAP, Lottie, Three.js) into deterministic MP4 videos — 'Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents.' A video is an HTML file whose elements carry timing/track attributes; the renderer seeks each frame in headless Chrome and encodes with FFmpeg. Ships agent skills/plugins for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI, a CLI, a free Studio app and ~450 reusable blocks. Requires Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg.
entries.fit_rationale: A strong programmatic-rendering fit for VyralX (and the renderer Hypit builds on). Constraint: headless-Chrome rendering is heavy for ~1GB servers — run renders on the owner's machine or post-ARM, not on the current fleet.

entries.name: LTX-2 / LTX-2.5 (Lightricks)
entries.what_it_does: The official Python inference and LoRA-training package for Lightricks' LTX-2.5 audio–video generative model (the legacy LTX-Video repo points here and is no longer actively developed). LTX-2.5 is a 22B DiT-based model generating synchronised audio+video from text/image/audio with native multi-shot generation; the repo provides multiple pipelines (distilled, production-quality, image-to-video, dubbing, etc.), ComfyUI integration and a trainer. Weights are gated Hugging Face downloads (~66 GiB).
entries.license: Code: Apache-2.0. Model weights: LTX-2.x Community License (free under $10M annual revenue; commercial licence above)
entries.fit_rationale: Reject for now on hardware alone: a 22B model with ~66GB of weights needs a serious GPU; the fleet has none and the free-tier rule rules out hosted generation APIs as a default. Revisit only if the owner gets GPU hardware. The open-source text/image-to-video idea stays on VyralX's list via lighter routes.

entries.name: VoiceStudio
entries.what_it_does: A free, fully-local, open-source voice studio billed as 'the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative': clone a voice from a short clean reference recording, design a voice from a text description, dub/translate videos with timed speech, dictate via a floating widget, transcribe, and narrate audiobooks — in 646 languages via its default engine (k2-fsa/OmniVoice, with dozens of other engines selectable). It runs entirely on the user's own hardware (Electron desktop app + local Python/FastAPI backend, Docker option), needs no account or API keys, and exposes a local API and MCP for agents/scripts.
entries.license: AGPL-3.0 for the app — BUT the default OmniVoice model weights are CC-BY-NC (non-commercial) per the repo's licence notice; per-engine licences vary; voice cloning requires the voice owner's permission
entries.fit_rationale: The corpus's local voice-cloning candidate for FRIDAY's voice. Runs on the owner's hardware, not the servers. Licence care is mandatory: the app is AGPL and the default engine's weights are non-commercial — fine for FRIDAY's private use, not for any commercial/public output without checking the chosen engine's licence. Gemini Live remains FRIDAY's voice engine; this is a TTS voice-source experiment.

entries.name: M3E Canvas
entries.what_it_does: A free, open-source, browser-only sketchpad for app screens built from real Material 3 Expressive components. You drag parts onto phone or desktop screens, link screens into tap/swipe navigation flows, preview the flow in-browser, theme it (palettes, light/dark, fonts, motion), then copy the whole design out as a concise natural-language prompt/brief (in English, Japanese, Chinese or Korean) for an AI coding tool (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor) to build the app. It generates no code itself; there is no backend — a static Next.js export in localStorage, hosted free on GitHub Pages.
entries.fit_rationale: Zero server cost and a direct implementation of the corpus's sketch-to-prompt front-end idea: the owner sketches, M3E Canvas emits the structured prompt, Forge builds from it. Usable today via its GitHub Pages hosting; nothing to run on the fleet.

entries.name: TradingAgents
entries.what_it_does: A multi-agent LLM framework that mirrors a real trading firm: four analysts (fundamentals, sentiment, news, technicals) report in parallel, bullish and bearish researchers debate their findings, a trader proposes a decision, a three-agent risk team argues over it, and a portfolio manager issues the final five-tier rating (Buy / Overweight / Hold / Underweight / Sell). Built on LangGraph with a persistent decision log and checkpoint resume. Research only — there is no broker integration and no order placement; a run ends with a rating and its reasoning.
entries.fit_rationale: The structured bull/bear debate with a risk-team veto and an auditable decision log is the pattern lesson for Stratex's signal review. It cannot run as-is on the fleet: it needs Python 3.11+ (fleet is 3.10), every decision burns 15+ LLM calls against free-tier quotas, and it has no execution layer and a US-equity focus, while Stratex trades Binance demo-fapi / OANDA practice with its own engine. Learn the debate-and-veto shape; do not integrate.

entries.name: Freqtrade
entries.what_it_does: A free, open-source crypto trading bot in Python: write strategies in Python, download exchange data, backtest, hyper-optimise parameters, and run dry-run or live on 30+ exchanges via CCXT (Binance, Bybit, Kraken, OKX, Gate, Hyperliquid and more, spot and selected futures). Includes FreqAI adaptive ML prediction models, a built-in WebUI, Telegram control, sqlite persistence, and lookahead/recursive-bias analysis tools for backtest hygiene.
entries.fit_rationale: The most battle-tested open-source crypto bot, and its dry-run → backtest → hyperopt discipline (plus the lookahead-analysis checks) is a model for Stratex's forward-measurement rig. As a runtime it does not fit: the project's own minimum is 2GB RAM (the whole VM has ~956MB, per-service cap ~180MB), it needs Python 3.12+ (fleet is 3.10), and adopting it would replace Stratex's own engine rather than extend it. Study the workflow and the FreqAI retraining pattern; do not run it.

entries.name: VectorBT
entries.what_it_does: A vectorized backtesting and quantitative-research library for Python: market data, indicators and portfolio simulations are packed into NumPy/pandas arrays and accelerated with Numba (plus an optional Rust engine), so thousands of strategy/parameter combinations can be swept in one run instead of looped one at a time. Includes portfolio analytics (trades, drawdowns, Sharpe/Sortino, QuantStats integration), walk-forward/robustness testing and interactive Plotly visualisation. Research only — no order routing or live trading. The community edition is the free base; VectorBT PRO is a separate paid product that adds limit orders, leverage, parallelisation and 100+ further features.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 with Commons Clause (fair-code; the Commons Clause bars selling the software itself)
entries.fit_rationale: Build Stratex's offline parameter-sweep research on the community edition's vectorized pattern: it is a pip-installable library (not a service), free for internal use, and ideal for sweeping strategy parameters locally before anything reaches the forward record. Constraints: run sweeps off-fleet or on small universes only (vectorized grids are RAM-hungry and the fleet VMs have ~956MB), and never depend on PRO-only features (limit orders, leverage) — the fleet stays free-only.

entries.name: Backtrader
entries.what_it_does: A feature-rich, event-driven Python framework for backtesting and live trading: a Cerebro engine coordinates multiple data feeds, timeframes and strategies, with 122 built-in indicators, a broker simulator (market/limit/stop/bracket/OCO orders, slippage and commission schemes), sizers, schedulers, trading calendars and analyzers (Sharpe, SQN, TimeReturn). Data from CSV, pandas or online sources; live trading was built for Interactive Brokers, OANDA (REST) and Visual Chart. Self-contained with no external dependencies beyond optional plotting.
entries.fit_rationale: The Cerebro/analyzer design is the textbook reference for event-driven backtest structure, and it is genuinely light (no dependencies, runs on Python 3.10). But building on an unmaintained GPL-3.0 framework whose pandas/NumPy compatibility is drifting — when Stratex already has its own engine — would import maintenance debt for no new capability. Read it for patterns; do not integrate.

entries.name: Hummingbot
entries.what_it_does: An open-source framework for designing and deploying automated crypto trading bots, specialised in market making and arbitrage across 140+ centralised and decentralised venues. Three strategy generations coexist: single-file Scripts, reusable V2 Controllers with self-contained Executors that manage an order lifecycle (position, DCA, grid, arbitrage, cross-exchange market making/XEMM, TWAP, liquidity provision — the position executor uses triple-barrier risk controls), and legacy V1 strategies (Pure Market Making, Avellaneda, Cross-Exchange Market Making). Standardised REST/WebSocket connectors per exchange, paper-trading connectors that simulate against live order books, and an `hbot` CLI / Docker deployment.
entries.fit_rationale: The V2 executor pattern (one component owning an order's full lifecycle, triple-barrier exits on the position executor) is a strong design lesson for Stratex's order management. Market making itself is out of scope: Stratex runs directional strategies on demo venues with no market-making mandate, no quoting capital and no latency budget, and the full client (conda/Docker stack) is far beyond the ~180MB per-service cap. Learn the executor lifecycle; do not adopt the runtime.

entries.name: CCXT
entries.what_it_does: A unified trading-API library covering 100+ cryptocurrency exchanges and prediction markets (Binance, Bybit, OKX, Kraken, Hyperliquid, Polymarket, Kalshi and more) behind one consistent interface for market data, balances, orders and positions, over REST and WebSocket. Written once in TypeScript and transpiled to Python, JavaScript, C#, PHP, Go, Java and Rust, so the same method names and return structures work in every language. It is a library, not a bot: no engine, no backtester, no daemon — code you import. Also ships a CLI and an MCP server.
entries.language: TypeScript (source of truth; Python and other language builds generated from it)
entries.fit_rationale: The one name in this list Stratex can genuinely build on: use the Python build selectively when adding a new crypto venue, instead of hand-rolling another exchange client, and copy its unified-API shape for Stratex's own venue layer. Limits: it does not cover OANDA (Stratex's FX venue), the working direct Binance integration should not be churned for its own sake, and on builder-code exchanges CCXT routing can add a ~1bp fee on top of exchange fees — check per-venue before routing real flow through it.

entries.name: FinRL
entries.what_it_does: The first open-source framework for financial reinforcement learning, from the AI4Finance Foundation: market data downloaders (Yahoo Finance, Alpaca, Binance, CCXT, WRDS and others), Gymnasium-style trading environments for stocks, crypto and portfolio allocation, and deep-RL agents (A2C, DDPG, PPO, SAC, TD3 via Stable-Baselines3, ElegantRL or RLlib) arranged in a train → test → trade pipeline. This repo is now the preserved classic/educational edition; the maintainers direct production work to the successor FinRL-X / FinRL-Trading stack.
entries.fit_rationale: Its environment/reward design (state features, turbulence index, transaction-cost modelling in the Gym env) is the reference if Stratex ever opens an RL research track. Training DRL agents is compute work the fleet cannot host — no GPU and ~956MB RAM per VM, against a PyTorch/Stable-Baselines3 stack — and several data sources it wires in are paid or account-gated (WRDS, premium feeds), against the free-only rule. Stratex's current programme is rule-based forward measurement; RL is premature. Read the env design; do not integrate.

entries.name: Lumibot
entries.what_it_does: A Python framework for building, backtesting and deploying trading strategies across stocks, options, futures, forex, crypto and prediction markets: the same Strategy class runs against historical data, then paper or live through a broker — Alpaca, Interactive Brokers, Tradier, Schwab, Tradovate, ProjectX, Bitunix, Polymarket, and crypto exchanges via CCXT. Supports three strategy styles — hand-written Python rules, LLM-agent strategies that research and place orders, and hybrids where an agent advises but Python sizes and submits (research agents can be set `allow_trading=False`). Ships free point-in-time SEC fundamentals for backtests; the vendor's recommended deep-history data sources (ThetaData, Polygon) are paid services, and a hosted BotSpot cloud/marketplace sits alongside the open-source library.
entries.fit_rationale: The backtest = paper = live single-strategy-class discipline and the hybrid guardrail (agent proposes with `allow_trading=False`, deterministic code executes) are patterns worth copying into Stratex. Adopting it would duplicate Stratex's existing engine, its broker set is US-centric (no OANDA, Binance only indirectly via CCXT), and serious backtesting leans on paid data — against the free-only rule. Learn the guardrail pattern; do not integrate.

entries.name: Polymarket API (official Python SDK: py-sdk)
entries.what_it_does: "Polymarket API" as named in the video is not a repository — it is the venue's three public HTTP APIs: the Gamma API (market/event catalogue, no auth), the Data API (wallet positions and trade history, no auth) and the CLOB API (live order books and pricing publicly; placing/cancelling orders requires a signed API key), documented at docs.polymarket.com, with trades settling on Polygon. This card records the official GitHub presence: Polymarket's unified Python SDK (`pip install polymarket-client`), one workflow-oriented client spanning public data, authenticated account, trading and wallet operations. It supersedes the older official Python client, Polymarket/py-clob-client (~1,230 stars, MIT), which is now archived and explicitly non-functional since the CLOB V2 migration — do not use it. The Polymarket org also publishes TypeScript/Rust CLOB clients, a Rust CLI and an agents framework.
entries.fit_rationale: The usable part for FRIDAY is the free, unauthenticated read-only Gamma/Data APIs: live prediction-market probabilities are a legitimate forecasting signal for Futuris, readable with plain HTTP if ever wired in — no SDK adoption needed today. Trading through the CLOB is out of scope: it is a real-money venue (no demo mode), access is geo-restricted by IP, and Stratex's mandate is demo-only measurement on Binance/OANDA. Record the APIs and the current SDK; integrate nothing.

entries.name: Claude Ads (AgriciDaniel)
entries.what_it_does: A free, open-source skill/plugin for Claude Code that turns the host agent into a paid-media auditor: source-grounded audits, strategy, creative briefs and monitoring across 12 ad platforms (Google, Meta, YouTube, LinkedIn, TikTok, Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Reddit, Pinterest, Snapchat, X). It reads account data/exports you supply and reports pass/fail/unknown findings with evidence; account changes stay drafts unless a capability gate passes. Ships a Python core (`claude_ads_core`), per-platform skills and an optional local Cockpit workbench. Upstream flags itself a "development candidate" — all 12 account-health scoring profiles are currently disabled.
entries.fit_rationale: Nothing to deploy on the fleet: it is a lightweight operator-side skill (Markdown + Python) that runs in a coding-agent host, so the ~180MB service caps don't apply. Its audit-checklist and evidence-gated draft pattern adapts directly to VyralX promotion work if/when the owner runs ads for the channel. Caveats: no ad accounts exist yet, upstream is pre-release with scoring disabled, and audits are only as good as the account data fed to them.

entries.name: Fincept Terminal
entries.what_it_does: A native desktop financial-research terminal pitched as a free Bloomberg alternative: C++20/Qt6 UI with embedded Python 3.11 analytics in a single binary. The open build includes DCF/portfolio/VaR analytics and an 18-module QuantLib suite, 37 AI trader/economist agents (BYO LLM key), 100+ data connectors (FRED, IMF, World Bank, Yahoo, Kraken, Polygon…), a paper-trading engine with 16 broker integrations, a visual node editor and MCP tools. The actively developed Enterprise edition is closed-source and paid ($15–45/user/mo); real-time data and multi-agent research are reserved for it, and the open repo now ships only one release a month.
entries.fit_rationale: A Qt6 desktop GUI cannot run on the headless ~956MB fleet VMs, its best features sit behind the paid Enterprise edition (breaks the FREE-only rule), and AGPL-3.0 copyleft bars embedding its code into FRIDAY services. Worth keeping as a UI/module-layout reference for a future Futuris/Stratex research desk (desk organisation, connector breadth, node-editor automation), not as code or a deployment.

entries.name: Vibe-Trading (HKUDS)
entries.what_it_does: HKU Data Science Lab's open-source personal trading agent: natural-language prompts become market research reports, runnable backtests and paper portfolios across equities (CN/HK/US and more), crypto, futures and forex, fed by 29 built-in free data sources with fallback. Ships a library of ~478 testable alpha factors (Alpha Zoo), multi-agent "investment committee" research teams, an MCP/API surface, a FastAPI + React web UI, and ~50 broker profiles (most paper-only; live execution is explicitly experimental and mandate-gated). Published on PyPI as `vibe-trading-ai`; still pre-1.0 (v0.1.x) and moving fast.
entries.fit_rationale: Direct deployment is out: it requires Python 3.11+ (fleet is 3.10) and the full FastAPI/React/agent stack is far over the ~180MB service cap. What adapts is the research layer: the MIT alpha-factor library, the plain-English backtest workflow and the committee-style research pattern are direct inputs to Stratex's demo-first measurement programme, to be mined selectively and run off-fleet or post-ARM. Its own warnings stand: live trading is unvalidated upstream, and the +243.6% figure in the carousel is a backtest screenshot, not a forward record.

entries.name: Camofox Browser (jo-inc)
entries.what_it_does: An anti-detection headless browser server for AI agents, built on Camoufox — a Firefox fork that spoofs fingerprints (hardware concurrency, WebGL, AudioContext, screen geometry, WebRTC) at the C++ engine level rather than with JS shims. It wraps that engine in a REST API (plus MCP/OpenClaw tool surfaces with full HTTP parity): accessibility snapshots ~90% smaller than raw HTML, stable element refs for clicking, per-session cookie/storage isolation, search macros for common sites, YouTube transcript extraction via yt-dlp, and VNC interactive login. Lazy launch + idle shutdown keeps it at ~40MB when idle; first run downloads a ~300MB Camoufox binary.
entries.fit_rationale: The idle footprint and on-demand lazy launch suit the fleet, and the snapshot/ref API is a better agent-browsing pattern than raw Playwright for IntelX research and FRIDAY web tasks. Constraints: an actively rendering Firefox will exceed the ~180MB service cap, so run it as an on-demand sidecar (or on the owner's machine / post-ARM), not an always-on service; the ~300MB binary is a real disk cost on the tiny VMs; and anti-detection browsing must stay within target sites' terms.

entries.name: Open Generative AI (Anil-matcha)
entries.what_it_does: A self-hosted, MIT-licensed studio (Next.js web app + Electron desktop) that puts 800+ hosted generative models (Flux, Midjourney-style, Kling, Sora, Veo, Seedream…) behind one interface across 14 sub-studios — Image Studio, Video Studio, Lip Sync, Cinema, Workflows and more — marketed as an uncensored, no-subscription alternative to Higgsfield, Freepik, Krea and OpenArt. The catch is in the plumbing: cloud generation runs through the paid, credit-metered MuAPI gateway with your own key, and the only fully free path is local inference in the desktop app via sd.cpp (images) or Wan2GP (video), which needs a real GPU. This single repo is also the project the carousels named two other ways: its "Image Studio" is a sub-studio of this repo, and "Open Higgsfield AI" was the project's earlier name (Open-Higgsfield-AI) before the rename to Open-Generative-AI.
entries.fit_rationale: The studio shell is free and MIT, but using it means paying MuAPI per generation (paid dependency — breaks the FREE-only rule; white-label hosting starts at $49/mo), and the free local engines need a GPU the fleet doesn't have; a Next.js/Electron studio also doesn't fit the ~180MB headless services. Keep as a UI reference only: the multi-studio layout is a useful pattern for a future VyralX creation console. The "200+ models locally, no subscriptions" carousel claim does not survive contact with the README.

entries.name: AutoHedge (The Swarm Corporation)
entries.what_it_does: An "enterprise-grade autonomous agent hedge fund" built on the Swarms multi-agent framework: five specialised LLM agents chained like a fund's org chart — Director (thesis), Quant (numeric validation), Risk Manager (position sizing), Execution Trader (orders) and Sentiment Analyst — running end-to-end market analysis and trade execution with minimal human input. In practice the only fully supported venue is Solana (via the Jupiter API, using a wallet private key); Coinbase is listed as in development. Beta software (v0.1.x on PyPI as `autohedge`), with no paper-trading/simulation mode described and no test suite. Not to be confused with virattt/ai-hedge-fund, a different, larger project.
entries.fit_rationale: The role-specialised agent pipeline (thesis → quant check → risk sizing → execution) is a useful reference mirror for Stratex's own design, and it is Python 3.10-compatible and MIT. Nothing else transfers: Solana memecoin execution is irrelevant to Stratex's Binance/OANDA demo programme, there is no demo/paper safety mode, it demands a live wallet key, and the repo has been stale since spring 2026. Pattern reference only; do not run it.

entries.name: Toprank (nowork-studio — now NotFair plugin)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source Claude Code plugin (15 skills, one per task) for SEO and Google Ads work: it connects to Google Search Console, PageSpeed Insights and the Google Ads API to audit a site against ~90 days of real traffic data, find keyword cannibalisation, duplicate-homepage and title/intent mismatches and missing structured data — then commits the fixes directly to the codebase rather than only reporting them. Also does keyword research (its "gap score" hunts keywords whose current top pages are weak), RSA ad-copy generation, Google Ads audits, a `/content-writer` agent for E-E-A-T content, and publishing to WordPress/Strapi/Contentful/Ghost. It doubles as a funnel to the company's hosted NotFair product (formerly named Toprank), which some workflows use.
entries.fit_rationale: Like Claude Ads, it is an operator-side plugin of skills, not a fleet service, so the VM caps don't bite: its Search-Console-grounded audit-and-fix workflow adapts directly to keeping the FRIDAY website (and VyralX content pages) search-healthy, using only the free local skills. Caveats: it needs a Search Console property with real traffic to be worth anything, auto-committed fixes must stay review-gated, and the hosted NotFair upsell paths are out under the FREE-only rule.

entries.name: Agentic Inbox (Cloudflare)
entries.what_it_does: Cloudflare's open-source, self-hosted email client with a built-in AI agent, running entirely on your own Cloudflare account — Workers, Durable Objects (isolated per-mailbox storage), R2 and Workers AI, built with the Cloudflare Agents SDK. The agent receives mail, classifies it, extracts summaries and drafts replies, with human approval before anything is sent. It is positioned as a data-sovereign alternative to paid AI email clients like Superhuman ($30/mo): your mail never leaves infrastructure you control.
entries.fit_rationale: The deployable itself cannot come to the fleet: it is hard-wired to Cloudflare Workers/Durable Objects/R2, a platform FRIDAY doesn't run on, and it has been unmaintained since Apr 2026. What adapts is the workflow pattern — classify → summarise → draft, human-approval-before-send, per-mailbox isolation — which maps cleanly onto FRIDAY's existing Gmail access and is exactly the triage behaviour the owner wants from his inbox. Adopt the pattern in FRIDAY, not the Workers stack.

entries.name: ClawRouter (BlockRunAI)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source, local LLM router built for autonomous agents (born in the OpenClaw ecosystem): an OpenAI-compatible proxy that analyses each request across 15 dimensions and routes it to the cheapest capable model in under 1ms, entirely locally, across ~91 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, DeepSeek and others. Its signature pieces are agent-native billing — no signup or API key, the agent pays per request in USDC via the x402 micropayment protocol from its own wallet (a credit-card-funded BlockRun API key also works) — and a 7-layer, agent-aware token-compression pipeline (deduplication, dictionary/path codebooks, JSON compaction and tool-observation summarisation) claiming 15–40% typical token savings. Distributed as the npm package `@blockrun/clawrouter`; 8 open-weight models are free forever.
entries.fit_rationale: The routing/compression ideas are genuinely relevant to Inference, but the product is a front door to BlockRun's paid gateway: beyond the 8 free models, every call is metered spend (USDC or card top-up), which breaks the FREE-only rule, and Inference already routes through free-tier keys with OmniRoute/FreeLLMAPI-class tooling carded in wave 1. Keep as a reference for the token-compression layer design (especially tool-observation summarisation) if Inference's context costs ever need cutting; do not adopt the gateway.

entries.name: Agent Memory (agentmemory)
entries.what_it_does: Persistent memory server for AI coding agents. Native hooks/plugins capture what an agent does in a session (file edits, tool calls, decisions), compress it into searchable memory, and inject relevant context at the start of the next session. Hybrid recall — BM25 keyword search works keyless with no API key, local embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) or a remote provider add semantic search, plus a knowledge graph. One local server (REST :3111, viewer :3113, 54 MCP tools, 17 native skills) shared across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, Hermes, OpenClaw and other MCP clients. Requires Node.js 20+.
entries.fit_rationale: Same observer/capture-compress-inject pattern as claude-mem (already carded), and a concrete design input for Memora: keyless BM25-first recall, 4-tier consolidation, secret scrubbing and session handoff are directly reusable ideas. It is a Node/TypeScript local coding-agent server, not a Python fleet service, so it cannot drop into the ~180 MB / Python 3.10 fleet — adapt the pattern into Memora rather than running it on the VMs.

entries.name: Scientific Agent Skills
entries.what_it_does: An open library of 177 ready-to-use Agent Skills (the reel said "160+") that turn any Agent Skills-compatible host (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Antigravity) into a research assistant. Each skill is a directory with a versioned SKILL.md plus references/scripts, covering genomics, cheminformatics/drug discovery, proteomics, clinical research, medical imaging, neuroscience, materials/physics, data analysis & visualisation, laboratory automation, scientific communication, research methodology, and access to 100+ scientific databases. Described in arXiv:2609.00065; no runtime server — the consuming agent executes the skills.
entries.fit_rationale: FRIDAY has no genomics, chemistry or clinical workload, so the bulk of the library has no fleet consumer. What transfers is the packaging discipline (versioned SKILL.md, references loaded on demand, skill-spec validation in CI) and a handful of research-methodology / data-analysis / literature-synthesis skills Futuris could cherry-pick. Do not install the full set: its per-skill Python stacks are built for desktop research hosts, not the 956 MB fleet.
entries.friday_agent_raw: Futuris (research methodology only); NONE for the wet-lab/science majority

entries.name: Diagram Design
entries.what_it_does: An Agent Skill (by Cathryn Lavery) that makes a coding agent produce editorial-quality diagrams instead of generic rounded-box output. 45 diagram types in the GitHub description (README now claims 50) — architecture, flowchart, sequence, quadrant, pyramid and more — each shipped in three variants (minimal light, minimal dark, full-editorial) as one self-contained HTML file with inline SVG: no build step, no JavaScript, no external images. It can match a brand's palette/fonts by reading a website, redraw Mermaid / draw.io / Excalidraw / PlantUML sources, and export to SVG or PNG. Installable as a Claude Code / Codex / Copilot / Cursor plugin or via `npx skills add cathrynlavery/diagram-design`. There is no application or server — the repo is Markdown reference files, example HTML and a few scripts; the "taste" (4px grid, 1px hairlines, no shadows) is written down as loadable instructions.
entries.fit_rationale: Zero runtime cost and nothing to host: it is a skill file-set the build/design workflow loads on demand, and its output is exactly what Website-UI and FRIDAY's docs need (brand-matched architecture and explainer diagrams as single HTML files). MIT and free. The one caveat from its own README: for diagrams that live in Git and change every sprint, Mermaid still diffs better — use Diagram Design for published diagrams.

entries.name: Anthropic Cybersecurity Skills
entries.what_it_does: The largest open-source cybersecurity skills library for AI agents: 818 structured skills (GitHub title says 817) across 34 security domains — cloud security, SOC operations, threat hunting, threat intelligence, web/API security, forensics, IAM, malware analysis, incident response, DevSecOps and more — each following the agentskills.io open standard (SKILL.md + optional Python scripts) and mapped to six frameworks: MITRE ATT&CK v19.1, NIST CSF 2.0, MITRE ATLAS, MITRE D3FEND, NIST AI RMF and MITRE Fight Fraud Framework (F3). Works with Claude Code, Copilot, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and 20+ platforms via `npx skills add mukul975/Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills`. Despite the name it is an independent community project by Mahipal Jangra (mukul975), explicitly not affiliated with Anthropic PBC, and it includes offensive/dual-use skills (red-team C2, phishing simulation, exploitation) flagged "authorized use only" in its own README.
entries.fit_rationale: A ready-made playbook library for Sentinel: cherry-pick the defensive skills (cloud/fleet hardening, SOC playbooks, threat hunting, vulnerability management, AI-security / prompt-injection checks) and map them onto Sentinel's audit and watchdog work, using the ATT&CK/CSF mappings as the checklist structure. Do not import the set wholesale — the offensive/red-team skills have no place in an always-on fleet agent, and each adopted skill's script needs review before it runs anywhere near production.

entries.name: Awesome Harness Engineering
entries.what_it_does: A curated awesome-list for "harness engineering" — the discipline of designing the scaffolding around a model (the runtime that turns a model into an agent: agent loop, tool interfaces, context delivery & compaction, planning artifacts, skills & MCP, permissions & authorization, memory & state, task runners & orchestration, verification loops & CI, observability & tracing, debugging, human-in-the-loop, sandboxes). Organised into Foundations, Design Primitives, Reference Implementations, Security/Sandbox/Permissions, Evals & Verification, Templates and Production Infrastructure, with links to the tools, patterns and essays in each area. It is a reading list, not software: the repo is Markdown plus a small Python URL-checker (`verify_urls.py`).
entries.license: Other (NOASSERTION on GitHub; a LICENSE file is present in the repo)
entries.language: None — curated Markdown list (Python helper script)
entries.fit_rationale: There is nothing to install, and that is the point: it is a syllabus for exactly the problems FRIDAY's orchestration keeps hitting (context compaction, permission boundaries, verification loops, observability, runaway-loop failure modes). Use it as the design reference when hardening FRIDAY's harness and Forge's build loops; adopt individual tools it lists only after their own verification.

entries.name: Open Viking (OpenViking)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source "context database for AI agents" from Volcengine (ByteDance). It unifies everything an agent knows — resources (docs, repos, web pages), memories (preferences, experience extracted when a session is committed) and skills — in one virtual filesystem addressed by `viking://` URIs, browsed with ordinary file operations (`ls`, `tree`, `read`, `find`, `grep`) instead of opaque vector queries. Every directory carries generated summaries in three loading tiers (L0 one-sentence abstract, L1 overview, L2 full source) so agents scan cheap summaries before loading content, and semantic search can be scoped to a directory subtree. Runs as a server (Python 3.10+, needs an embedding model and a VLM provider — Volcengine/OpenAI/Kimi/GLM or local Ollama) with CLI (`ov`), Python/Go/TypeScript SDKs, an MCP endpoint and plugins for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Hermes, OpenCode and others. Self-reported LoCoMo results: 80–83% memory accuracy vs 24–57% native, with 34–91% fewer input tokens. A hosted Volcengine edition also exists (first 50 files free).
entries.license: AGPL-3.0 (core server; CLI crates and examples Apache-2.0)
entries.language: Python (with C++ vector engine, Rust crates, Go/TypeScript SDKs)
entries.fit_rationale: The design ideas are strong for Memora (one inspectable filesystem for memory + knowledge + skills, L0/L1/L2 tiered loading, directory-scoped search, sessions committed as readable Markdown), but the thing itself cannot run on the fleet: it is a full context server with its own vector engine that expects a VLM + embedding provider, far beyond a ~180 MB service budget on a 956 MB VM, and its AGPL-3.0 core is the most restrictive licence in this set. Memora's store decision is already settled (Redis/Qdrant, provisioned after the ARM server) — borrow the tiering and inspectability, don't integrate the server.

entries.name: Karpathy Skill (Andrej Karpathy Skills)
entries.what_it_does: A single ~65-line `CLAUDE.md` file — not a skill pack and not code. Forrest Chang (Jiayuan Chang) distilled Andrej Karpathy's January 2026 post on LLM coding pitfalls into four behavioural principles for coding agents: (1) Think Before Coding — state assumptions, surface tradeoffs, don't pick an interpretation silently; (2) Simplicity First — minimum code, no speculative abstractions; (3) Surgical Changes — touch only what the task requires, no drive-by refactors; (4) Goal-Driven Execution — turn tasks into verifiable success criteria and loop until verified. The repo also packages the same text as a Claude Code plugin (`karpathy-guidelines` skill) and a Cursor rule. Karpathy wrote the observations, not the file; he did not publish or endorse this repo.
entries.license: MIT (declared in the README/plugin manifests; note the repo has no LICENSE file, so GitHub shows no detected licence)
entries.language: None — Markdown only, no runtime, no dependencies
entries.fit_rationale: The cheapest item in the whole corpus: one instruction file, zero cost, zero footprint, and its four principles are already FRIDAY's working rules in spirit (state assumptions, surgical PRs, verify against success criteria before claiming done). Drop the principles into the repo's agent instruction files (CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md equivalents) for Forge and the collaborator crews. It is a mitigation, not a cure — Karpathy's own post noted CLAUDE.md instructions alone had not fixed these failure modes — so it complements, never replaces, independent verification.

entries.name: Graphify
entries.what_it_does: Turns any codebase — plus its docs, SQL schemas, configs and PDFs — into a queryable knowledge graph, exposed to coding agents as a `/graphify` skill (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot and 20+ other assistants). Pass one is deterministic and fully local: tree-sitter AST parsing across ~40 languages extracts classes, functions, imports, calls and inheritance with no LLM and nothing leaving the machine. Pass two (optional, spends model tokens) extracts concepts from docs/PDFs/images/video transcripts. The merged NetworkX graph is persisted as `graphify-out/` — `graph.json`, a `GRAPH_REPORT.md` of key concepts and surprising connections, and an interactive `graph.html` — and queried with `query` / `path` / `explain` instead of grepping file by file. Every edge is tagged EXTRACTED or INFERRED with a confidence trail; there is no vector store. Official PyPI package is `graphifyy` (double-y — the README warns other graphify* packages are unaffiliated). A paid Graphify Cloud sibling offers always-on/cross-repo graphs.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (relicensed from MIT in July 2026; LICENSE-MIT retained for pre-relicense portions)
entries.fit_rationale: One of the few heavyweight names that fits the fleet exactly as-is: Python 3.10+ (the fleet's version), a local on-demand CLI rather than a resident service (zero idle RAM), and the code pass costs no LLM credits. Run it per-agent subfolder on the FRIDAY repo (the skill itself warns past ~500 files / 2M words, and the repo is ~5,300 files, so graph each agent separately) to give Forge and the review crews a caller/dependency map instead of blind grepping. Skip Graphify Cloud (paid) and leave the token-spending doc/media semantic pass off by default.
entries.friday_agent_raw: Forge; Cortex / Memora (secondary consumers of the graph)

entries.name: Open Code Review (Alibaba)
entries.what_it_does: Alibaba's internal AI code-review assistant, open-sourced. A CLI (`ocr`, installed via `npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`) with a hybrid architecture: deterministic engineering — not the model — decides which files get reviewed, how related files are bundled into isolated sub-agent review units, and which rules apply to each file (built-in multi-language ruleset covering NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection and more); an LLM agent with tool use then makes only the judgement call and produces structured, line-level comments on Git diffs, branch ranges, single commits, or whole files (`ocr scan`). Works with any OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible endpoint (20+ provider presets including Gemini, OpenRouter, DeepSeek), or in Delegation Mode where a host coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Kimi Code, Copilot CLI) runs the review with its own model and OCR supplies file selection and rules — no separate API key. Ships CI recipes for GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, GitFlic and Gerrit, with JSON/SARIF output. Requires Git ≥ 2.41. On Alibaba's own AACR-Bench (50 repos, 200 PRs, 1,505 annotated issues) it claims higher precision and F1 than Claude Code with the same model at ~1/9 the tokens, with deliberately lower recall; the benchmark is the vendor's own and not independently replicated.
entries.fit_rationale: It slots straight into FRIDAY's PR-based workflow as a tool, not a service: a Go CLI run locally or in GitHub Actions on each PR, adding a deterministic first review pass (file selection can't skip files, security rules flag SQLi/XSS) before the independent human-style review the merge queue already requires. No resident memory, no fleet hosting, free apart from the LLM endpoint — use Delegation Mode or the fleet's existing free providers to keep it at zero added cost. Two limits to keep explicit: its recall is deliberately low, so it supplements and never replaces the existing review step, and its headline benchmark is Alibaba's own.

entries.name: Social Media Research Skills (ScrapeCreators)
entries.what_it_does: A pack of 13 AI-agent skills (Agent Skills spec — Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, Copilot, etc.) for social-media research across TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, Reddit, X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Threads, Bluesky, Pinterest and ad libraries: outlier-post finder, transcript intelligence, comment mining, competitor teardown, ad-library teardown, trend discovery, influencer prospecting, audience research, social-listening brief, product-demand research, creator-profile teardown and content repurposing. All data comes from the hosted ScrapeCreators API (`SCRAPECREATORS_API_KEY` required); the skills themselves are the workflow/report layer on top of it.
entries.fit_rationale: The workflow designs are exactly VyralX's hook/competitor research job (steal hooks from top posts + rivals, per the source carousel) and are worth copying as patterns against FRIDAY's own free Instagram/social connectors. The skills themselves cannot be adopted: their only data layer is the paid ScrapeCreators API — 100 free lifetime credits, then pay-as-you-go packs ($47 for 25,000 credits, $497 for 500,000, checked 2026-11-16) — which breaks the fleet's FREE-only rule for any sustained use.

entries.name: Local Deep Research (LearningCircuit)
entries.what_it_does: A self-hosted, privacy-first deep-research assistant that turns a question into a cited report: it searches 10+ engines (web/SearXNG, arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, plus private documents), synthesises with a local or cloud LLM, and builds an encrypted (SQLCipher) personal knowledge library from the sources it finds. Modes include a LangGraph agentic strategy, quick pipelines, news/research subscriptions, an HTTP/Python API and an MCP server. Headline claim ~95% SimpleQA — achieved with Qwen3.6-27B running locally on an RTX 3090. Default install is Docker/pip plus Ollama and SearXNG alongside it.
entries.fit_rationale: Adapt its research pattern into IntelX, not the deployment: borrow the multi-engine routing, LangGraph agentic search strategy and cited-report synthesis, but drive it with Inference's free-tier cloud LLMs and free search sources. Do not self-host the full stack on the fleet — the documented local path needs Ollama with a 20B+ model (3090-class GPU for its benchmark), a separate SearXNG instance and its own web/DB app, far beyond a ~956MB VM / ~180MB-per-service cap.

entries.name: OpenCreator (KrillinAI)
entries.what_it_does: Formerly KrillinAI, the video translation/dubbing tool for 120+ languages. Now an open-source desktop/web AI workspace for creators, powered by OpenAI Codex CLI as its agent engine: video downloader (YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Bilibili, X, etc.), video translation with subtitle editing, dubbing and portrait/landscape rendering, plus thumbnail/image generation, article and short-video-script writing, stick-figure animation and text-to-speech — ten creator tools, reusable Skills and creation templates in one local workspace (Node.js 22+, pnpm, desktop app or web-from-source).
entries.fit_rationale: A useful reference for VyralX's all-in-one creator pipeline, especially the proven KrillinAI chain (transcribe → translate subtitles → dub → portrait render) and its Skills/template layout. Not adoptable on the fleet: it is a desktop-first Codex-CLI workspace, not a headless service for a ~956MB VM, and its image/video generation depends on paid third-party model APIs (GPT Image, Seedream/Kling Image, Seedance/Kling/Veo) — against the FREE-only rule.

entries.name: FLUX.2 (Black Forest Labs)
entries.what_it_does: The official *inference code* repo for Black Forest Labs' FLUX.2 image models — minimal Python code to run text-to-image generation and single/multi-reference image editing locally; the model weights themselves are separate Hugging Face downloads, not in this repo. Family: FLUX.2 [dev], a 32B-parameter model, and the faster FLUX.2 [klein] 4B / 9B (plus 9B KV and Base variants). Inference code was tested on GB200 with CUDA 12.9 and Python 3.12.
entries.license: Code: Apache-2.0. Model weights split by model — [klein] 4B, [klein] 4B Base and the FLUX.2 autoencoder: Apache-2.0; [klein] 9B, 9B KV, 9B Base and FLUX.2 [dev] (32B): FLUX Non-Commercial License / FLUX.2-dev Non-Commercial License (no commercial use of those weights/outputs under that licence)
entries.fit_rationale: Reject for the fleet on hardware and licence together. Weights/VRAM: [klein] 4B needs ~8GB VRAM (RTX 3090/4070-class consumer GPU); [dev] 32B needs an H100-equivalent GPU (an RTX 4090 only via quantisation + a remote text encoder). The fleet has no GPU and ~956MB RAM total, and runs Python 3.10 not 3.12/CUDA. Licence compounds it: only the 4B weights are Apache-2.0 — the higher-quality 9B and [dev] weights are non-commercial, unusable for VyralX's commercial content work, and the hosted BFL API alternative is paid (FREE-only rule). Revisit only if the owner gets GPU hardware, and then only the Apache-2.0 4B.

entries.name: ACE-Step 1.5 (ACE-Step)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source local music-generation foundation model — full original songs (10 seconds to 10 minutes, 50+ languages of lyrics, cover/repaint, vocal-to-BGM, track separation, LoRA personalisation) from a text prompt, via a hybrid architecture: a language model plans the song blueprint/lyrics and a Diffusion Transformer renders the audio. Ships a Gradio UI, REST API and CLI; claims commercial-grade quality, under 2 seconds per song on an A100 and under 10 seconds on an RTX 3090. Requires Python 3.11–3.12.
entries.fit_rationale: Reject on hardware alone, despite the clean MIT licence: even the smallest configuration (2B turbo, ~4.7GB of weights) is documented as needing under 4GB VRAM at best, with ≤6GB-VRAM use requiring INT8 quantisation + full CPU offload, and the XL 4B models need ~9GB of weights and ≥12GB VRAM (≥20GB recommended). The fleet has no GPU, ~956MB RAM per VM and Python 3.10 (the repo needs 3.11–3.12), so no variant can run there. Original-music generation for VyralX stays an idea to source elsewhere; revisit only with GPU hardware.

entries.name: Podcastfy
entries.what_it_does: An open-source Python alternative to NotebookLM's podcast feature: transforms multimodal content — websites, PDFs, images, YouTube videos, or a user-supplied topic — into engaging, multilingual two-host audio conversations with GenAI. Transcript generation via 100+ LLM models, audio via OpenAI / Google / ElevenLabs / Microsoft Edge TTS; usable as a Python package, CLI, or FastAPI service, with short (2–5 min) and longform (30+ min) modes.
entries.fit_rationale: The transcript→dialogue→TTS pattern is a clean fit for a VyralX audio/repurposing lane (article or video in, podcast-style audio out), and VyralX remains the maker/publisher (UNLISTED). Paid-API care: the default config needs `GEMINI_API_KEY` (transcript, default gemini-2.5-flash — the fleet's existing Gemini keys / free tier suffice) plus `OPENAI_API_KEY` for default TTS (paid — do not use). The repo's own config docs prove two free paths: Gemini-only (`geminimulti` TTS, one Gemini key) and a no-API-keys path (local LLM + Microsoft Edge TTS, free); ElevenLabs is optional/paid. Two blockers to adopting as-is: it requires Python 3.11+ (fleet is Python 3.10) and its FFmpeg/audio workload will not fit a ~180MB service cap on the ~956MB VMs — borrow the pipeline into VyralX and run it as a batch job post-ARM or on the owner's machine, not as a resident fleet service.

entries.name: OpenMontage
entries.what_it_does: Billed as the world's first open-source, agentic video production system: 12 production pipelines (animated explainer, animation, avatar spokesperson, cinematic, clip factory, documentary montage, hybrid, localization & dub, podcast repurpose, screen demo, talking head, character animation), 100+ tools and 700+ agent skill / production-knowledge files that turn an AI coding assistant into a full video studio — research, scripting, asset generation, editing and final composition, with scored provider selection, quality gates, budget controls and a live storyboard (Backlot) approval board. The agent is the orchestrator; composition is via Remotion (React) or HyperFrames (HTML/GSAP) plus FFmpeg.
entries.fit_rationale: The strongest production-system pattern in this carousel for VyralX: pipeline manifests, stage-director skills, scored provider selection, pre/post-render quality gates, budget governance and a storyboard approval gate are exactly what VyralX's own pipeline should copy, with VyralX remaining the maker and publishing staying UNLISTED. Its zero-API-key path is real (offline Piper TTS, Archive.org/NASA/Wikimedia footage, free-key Pexels/Unsplash/Pixabay, Remotion/HyperFrames + FFmpeg); all other providers (FAL, Kling, ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Runway, HeyGen, Suno — showcase videos cost ~$0.15–$5 each) are optional, not required. Not adoptable as-is on the fleet: Python 3.10+ matches, but the full stack (Node.js 22+, Remotion/headless rendering, optional Blender) far exceeds the ~956MB VMs and ~180MB/service caps, and its local video-generation path is GPU-only (Wan/Hunyuan/LTX — rejected for the fleet). Run any real OpenMontage renders off-fleet or post-ARM; AGPL-3.0 care if anything built from it is ever distributed.

entries.name: Short Video Factory (AI Short Video Factory)
entries.what_it_does: A cross-platform desktop app (Electron, Windows/macOS/Linux) for one-click generation of product-marketing and general-content short videos with AI batch auto-editing: prompt text + storyboard material in, finished shorts out. Integrates AI copywriting (any OpenAI-compatible API format), speech synthesis (EdgeTTS), automatic video mixing/editing, subtitle effects, multilingual support, and batch processing that keeps synthesising videos to a preset queue. Runs fully locally.
entries.fit_rationale: Its batch pattern is directly on-target for VyralX: prompt + storyboard material → copy → free EdgeTTS voice → auto mix/edit → subtitled shorts, queued in batches — borrow that batch-queue, auto-mix and subtitle-effects design for VyralX's own pipeline (VyralX makes the videos; publishing stays UNLISTED). No hard paid dependency: TTS is EdgeTTS (free) and copy generation accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so it can be pointed at a free-tier provider. Not adoptable on the fleet: it is a TypeScript/Electron desktop GUI, not a headless Python service, so it cannot run inside VyralX's ~180MB service cap on the ~956MB VMs — if run at all, it runs on the owner's machine; on the fleet only the pattern transfers. AGPL-3.0 care if anything built from it is ever distributed.

entries.name: AI YouTube Shorts Generator
entries.what_it_does: An open-source alternative to Opus Clip / Vidyo.ai / Klap / SubMagic: turns a long-form YouTube video (or a local file) into ranked, viral-ready 9:16 shorts — LLM highlight detection scored on hooks, emotional peaks, quotable lines and story peaks (each clip gets a viral score, hook line and reason), Whisper transcription, smart de-duplication of overlapping highlights, and automatic vertical cropping (face tracking in local mode). CLI + Python library, batch processing via a URL list, JSON output for downstream automation; no watermarks or per-clip credits in local mode.
entries.fit_rationale: The highlight-ranking framework (virality scoring + hook + reason per clip, dedupe, auto vertical crop) is a useful VyralX repurposing pattern for turning long videos into Shorts, with VyralX remaining the maker/publisher (UNLISTED). Mode restriction is mandatory under the FREE-only rule: the default `--mode api` requires a paid MuAPI key for download, transcription, ranking and cropping — reject that mode. The `--mode local` path avoids MuAPI entirely (yt-dlp + faster-whisper on CPU + FFmpeg/OpenCV) and needs only one LLM key for highlight ranking — Gemini (default gemini-2.5-flash, free tier suffices, fleet already holds Gemini keys) or OpenAI. Python 3.10+ matches the fleet, but local Whisper + video processing is heavy for ~956MB VMs — run tiny/base Whisper as an off-peak batch job or post-ARM, not as a resident service.

entries.name: Social Media Agent (LangChain)
entries.what_it_does: A LangGraph agent for sourcing, curating and scheduling social media posts with human-in-the-loop: give it a URL and it drafts a Twitter/X and LinkedIn post from the content, routes it through an Agent Inbox where a human can edit, accept or reject it, and can run on crons to ingest links (including from Slack) and schedule approved posts. Supports image selection/upload and style/prompt customisation.
entries.fit_rationale: Learn from the pattern, do not integrate. The human-in-the-loop inbox (draft → edit/accept/reject → schedule) and URL→post drafting flow are a good approval-gate model for VyralX's publishing workflow, where publishing stays UNLISTED and under owner/agent control. It fails FRIDAY's constraints on every other axis: a hard stack of paid/freemium APIs — Anthropic API is the LLM (paid, no free tier that suffices), FireCrawl for scraping (500 free credits, then paid), Arcade for social auth/scheduling, a LangSmith key required just to run the LangGraph server locally, and the full setup adds Google Vertex AI, Twitter and LinkedIn developer apps, Supabase and Slack; it targets X/LinkedIn text posts, not VyralX's YouTube-first video pipeline; and it is TypeScript/LangGraph, not a Python fleet service that could fit the ~180MB caps. Borrow the HITL pattern only.

entries.name: Lemo-Opuscar (Lemomo)
