entries.what_it_does: A Claude Code plugin/skill toolbox of film styles made entirely in code: each style is a `STYLE.md` prompt plus a demo film rendered frame-by-frame (canvas/WebGL pages, ffmpeg), with `DIRECTOR.md` (story, rhythm, camera) and `TECHNIQUE.md` (rendering, voice, music) guides, code-generated scores and TTS narration — no video model, no stock footage. The README's install line (`claude plugin marketplace add lemomo-ai/lemo-opuscar`) matches the Phase 1 lead verbatim. The library has grown since the slide: it now ships 99 styles in 15 categories (the slide and an Oct 2026 Medium write-up said 59).
entries.license: Other (NOASSERTION) — a `LICENSE` file plus a `LICENSES/` directory with REUSE-style per-part licensing; GitHub detects no single standard licence, so check the specific part before reusing it
entries.language: JavaScript / Python tooling (Claude Code plugin; Node + Python)
entries.fit_rationale: Running it needs Node 20+, ffmpeg 7+ and Python 3.11+ (the fleet is Python 3.10) and ~30–60 minutes of agent time per film; frame rendering is far too heavy for the ~956MB / ~180MB-per-service fleet. Its value to VyralX is as a style library: mine the `STYLE.md` prompts and gallery for looks to feed VyralX's own renderer.

entries.name: MG Styles 15 (Vincentwei1021)
entries.what_it_does: Fifteen motion-design styles, each a 10-second film Claude Opus 5.5 made by writing code from one prompt — picture (SVG/Canvas/WebGL/Three.js), animation, music and sound effects all code, no image/video generation. For every style it publishes the film, the style notes, the full prompt and the complete source, plus a headless-Chrome frame renderer (`harness/render.mjs`) and a Python audio-synthesis toolkit. Slide match is verbatim: the README's style 05 is "soft. — Soft Landing" and style 12 is "NEON DRIVE — Midnight 1986", both named in the Phase 1 slide description.
entries.language: HTML/JavaScript (films and renderer), with Python soundtrack scripts
entries.fit_rationale: The prompts are the asset: MIT-licensed, so the 15 prompt blocks can be copied straight into VyralX's prompt library as style references. Running its own harness needs Node 22, headless Chrome, Python 3.11+ and Blender for the 3D style — off-fleet work, not a fleet service.

entries.name: Claude Animation Base (JohnHeibel)
entries.what_it_does: A starter kit for animating hand-painted cartoons with Claude: p5.js + p5.brush code, the Clawd character with 31 acted emotions (views, eyes, mouths, hats, dances), an `ANIMATION_GUIDE.md` that briefs the model (storyboard first, handmade boiling-linework look, transitions always), and a headless-Chrome renderer that outputs MP4. It is the generalised base extracted from the author's PDoomVideo music video. The repo description — "hand-painted cartoons… Clawd character, 31 acted emotions" — matches the Phase 1 slide description verbatim.
entries.fit_rationale: A self-contained kit built around its own character, and the README itself warns p5.brush watercolour fills render at seconds per frame without a GPU — not viable on the fleet. The transferable parts for VyralX are the technique: the model-facing animation guide and the emotion/model-sheet approach for cartoon shorts.

entries.name: P(doom) Video — Lyric Music Video (mexicat)
entries.what_it_does: The full project of a code-rendered, karaoke-style lyric music video for the song "I'm Upping My P(doom)", built with Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code: a TypeScript + three.js renderer where every frame is a deterministic function of song time, word-synced lyric typography, and a Python analysis pipeline (Demucs stem separation, CTC forced alignment cross-checked with Whisper, beat/onset analysis) that produced the timing data. Renders identical 1080p60 or true 4K60 exports. This matches the Phase 1 slide on every distinctive point: lyric music video built entirely with code, three.js renderer, lyric timing tools, and a documented 4K render.
entries.license: MIT (code; the song, lyrics and fonts keep their own ownership/licences per the README credits)
entries.language: TypeScript (three.js, bun + Vite), with Python analysis tools
entries.fit_rationale: A single finished artwork, not a reusable tool, and far beyond fleet hardware: its own README puts a 4K render at ~57 minutes on an M5 Pro with ~23GB peak memory. The reusable lesson for VyralX music videos is the lyric-alignment pipeline (Demucs + CTC/Whisper timing → deterministic scene timeline).

entries.name: PDoomVideo — Cartoon Music Video (JohnHeibel)
entries.what_it_does: Source code for the hand-painted cartoon music video of "I'm Upping My P(doom)" (the same song as mexicat/pdoom-video, slide 4): nine chapters painted frame-by-frame in p5.js + p5.brush around the Clawd character, rendered via headless Chrome + ffmpeg. The README states "Everything in this repository was generated by the model" and that Opus wrote both the shot-by-shot `STORYBOARD.md` and the `ANIMATION_GUIDE.md` that briefed its subagents — matching the Phase 1 slide description ("painted with p5.js and p5.brush; everything generated by the model") verbatim in substance. This is the project ClaudeAnimationBase (slide 3) was later distilled from.
entries.license: None stated — no LICENSE file in the repo, so all rights reserved by default; study it, do not copy its code
entries.fit_rationale: A single finished artwork with no licence, so there is nothing to adopt or adapt legally. Its storyboard/guide workflow is already available in reusable, MIT-licensed form in the same author's ClaudeAnimationBase; treat this repo as the worked example behind that kit.

entries.name: LaunchVideo / shipvideo (diggerhq)
entries.what_it_does: "Paste a URL or a prompt, get a launch video": Claude Opus 5.5 writes a single HTML film (20–40 seconds), and a serverless agent on OpenComputer renders it frame-by-frame in headless Chromium and encodes it with ffmpeg (product name LaunchVideo, launchvideo.io). A small Next.js web app provides the form and download signing.
entries.license: None stated — no LICENSE file in the repo root and GitHub reports no licence
entries.fit_rationale: It runs on the external OpenComputer serverless platform with a paid Claude Opus API behind it, which breaks the fleet's free-only rule if used as-is, and it carries no licence. The URL → HTML-film → headless-render pattern is already covered for VyralX by the HyperFrames card.

entries.name: Awesome Claude 5.5 Videos (athemeroy)
entries.what_it_does: A source-linked catalogue of Claude 5.5 video workflows — Opus/Sonnet/Haiku demos (plus separately labelled creator-reported Fable items) organised by model, content domain and style, each entry tied to its original source post, with production evidence: inputs, revisions, task costs, and links to reusable open-source projects (it itself cross-links Lemo-Opuscar and ClaudeAnimationBase from this same slide set). The slide match is exact and numeric: the README states "As of 2026-10-11: 424 distinct source posts", matching the slide's "424 Claude Videos, Organized by Category".
entries.license: CC-BY-4.0 (original writing and charts; linked works and stills belong to their creators)
entries.language: Markdown / data collection (awesome list, with Python chart scripts)
entries.fit_rationale: A zero-runtime research catalogue: nothing to deploy, and nothing the fleet needs to run. Mine it when VyralX needs worked examples, per-category style evidence, or realistic cost/revision expectations for code-made videos. CC-BY-4.0 requires attribution if its text or charts are republished.

entries.name: Awesome Opus 5.5 Videos (yihui-dev)
entries.what_it_does: A collection of viral videos made with Claude Opus 5.5 — every one produced by asking the model to write the animation as code (HTML, Canvas, SVG, Three.js) — together with the prompt behind each video, organised into motion graphics, explainers, 3D scenes and games/interactive, with live remakes viewable on Skillry. The slide match is exact and numeric: the README states "703 prompts in `prompts/` and `data/videos.json`", matching the slide's "The Ultimate Prompt Library with 703 Prompts". Owner spelling resolved: the GitHub page itself is **yihui-dev**; the "yinhui-dev" spelling in one secondary summary is a misspelling.
entries.language: Markdown + JSON (prompt/data collection; no application code)
entries.fit_rationale: A prompt library, and a strong one for VyralX: 703 real, categorised prompts at zero runtime cost — copy the relevant ones (MIT) into VyralX's prompt references instead of inventing styles from scratch. Nothing in it runs on the fleet, and nothing needs to.

entries.name: OpenFilm
entries.what_it_does: An open-source AI video agent: a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex or any agent that can run a command) writes a film as plain web pages — one `film.html` whose tracks cut together pages, footage, stills and sound, each shot drawn by a `frame(t)` function — and renders it to MP4 via headless Chromium + FFmpeg. Ships Studio, a local browser editor with a real timeline where anything the agent made can be trimmed, moved, restyled or retyped by hand, plus a desktop app and a free built-in library of music, sounds, voices and templates. Generated voice/music/images/video are optional bring-your-own-key services; making, editing and rendering need no account. Install is `npx skills add openfilm/openfilm`; requires Node 22.2+ and FFmpeg (first run downloads ~100 MB of Chromium).
entries.license: MIT (the format, CLI, Studio and desktop app; the OpenFilm name and logo are trademarks)
entries.fit_rationale: The same HTML-as-video pattern VyralX already leans toward via HyperFrames, with a hand-editable Studio on top, which suits VyralX's approve-before-publish workflow. Constraint, same as HyperFrames: rendering is headless-Chromium work — too heavy to run inside a ~180 MB service on the ~956 MB fleet VMs; run renders on the owner's machine or post-ARM, with VyralX orchestrating. Very new (6 weeks old), so treat APIs as unstable.

entries.name: Nextwork AI Video Editor — "cooked."
entries.what_it_does: A Claude Code plugin (also usable via Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI and Copilot skill installs) that edits a talking-head video in the style of a creator you like. You give it your raw clip plus 3–6 reference videos that share one editing format; it measures their cut speed, zooms, captions, cards, graphics and sound into a saved, reusable **style**, cuts your video's retakes/false starts/pauses by transcript, then renders in that style (Remotion) through staged approvals — cut, look, render. Also makes Shorts from a long video/podcast link, a product video from a website URL, and a "creator teardown" that turns a profile into a style. Runs locally on your computer with a browser editor window; setup installs Python, FFmpeg, Node, a local Whisper transcription model and the renderer (~1.5 GB total). Optional free-to-start keys: ElevenLabs for verbatim transcripts, Gemini for reading a creator's visual look; local Whisper is the free default.
entries.language: Python (plugin skills/scripts) with a Node/Remotion renderer
entries.fit_rationale: The transferable idea for VyralX is the measured-style workflow: analyse a liked creator's format once into a reusable style profile, then apply it to VyralX's own footage with staged human approval — a good fit for the channel's talking-head/shorts output. Caveats: it is built around Claude Code, and its README states you need a Claude account with a paid plan or an API key to drive it, which conflicts with the fleet's free-only rule for unattended server use; and the ~1.5 GB local install plus Remotion rendering belong on the owner's machine, not the ~956 MB VMs. Adapt the style-analysis pattern into VyralX's existing pipeline rather than adopting the plugin wholesale.

entries.name: OpenVoice (MyShell / MIT)
entries.what_it_does: An instant voice-cloning audio foundation model built by MIT and MyShell researchers: it extracts the tone colour of a reference speaker from a short clip and applies it to speech generated in multiple languages and accents, with granular control over emotion, accent, rhythm, pauses and intonation, including zero-shot cross-lingual cloning (speak a language the reference speaker never spoke). V2 (April 2024) improves audio quality, natively supports English, Spanish, French, Chinese, Japanese and Korean, and uses MyShell's MeloTTS as its base TTS. It is a Python library with downloadable V1/V2 checkpoints and notebook demos — a model you embed in your own pipeline, not a finished app. This is the OpenVoice the source carousel means: its screenshot card is titled "OpenVoice — Versatile Instant Voice Cloning", which is the exact title of this project's paper (arXiv:2312.01479).
entries.license: MIT — both V1 and V2, free for commercial use (relicensed from CC-BY-NC in April 2024; some older third-party pages still show the old licence)
entries.fit_rationale: A genuinely free, commercially-usable voice-cloning engine is exactly what a faceless channel needs for a consistent narrator voice without ElevenLabs bills, and the MIT licence is clean. It cannot run on the fleet: it is a PyTorch model with separately downloaded checkpoints (plus MeloTTS for V2) — far beyond a ~180 MB service on a ~956 MB VM, and CPU inference is slow. Run it on the owner's hardware (or future GPU/ARM capacity) as an offline narration-rendering step whose MP3s VyralX then assembles, in the same pattern as the VoiceStudio card. Gemini Live remains FRIDAY's live voice; this is an offline TTS voice source.

entries.name: LongCat-Video + Avatar 1.5 (Meituan)
entries.what_it_does: Meituan LongCat team's open-source foundational video generation model (13.6B parameters) unifying text-to-video, image-to-video and video-continuation, designed for minutes-long generation without quality drift. The Avatar line is what the source carousel points at: LongCat-Video-Avatar turns audio (+ text, + an optional reference image) into lip-synced talking-character video, and Avatar 1.5 (May 2026) upgrades the audio encoder to Whisper-Large for accurate lip sync, adds full-body temporal stability and 8-step distilled fast inference, supporting single- and multi-character and even 5-minute-plus videos. (The repo has moved on since the carousel: Avatar 1.6 was released 2026-11-15.) Weights are separate multi-GB Hugging Face downloads; inference is PyTorch/CUDA with FlashAttention, documented in single- and multi-GPU `torchrun` configurations — independent hands-on testing ran it on a 40 GB NVIDIA A800, and only with INT8 quantisation plus distillation.
entries.fit_rationale: Reject on hardware alone, same as LTX-2: a 13.6B-parameter diffusion model needing a datacentre-class GPU (40 GB card in independent testing) and multi-GB weights cannot run anywhere in FRIDAY's world — the fleet is two ~956 MB-RAM VMs with no GPU, and the free-only rule rules out renting GPU generation as a default. The talking-avatar idea itself stays on VyralX's list via lighter routes; revisit only if the owner gets serious GPU hardware.

entries.name: MoneyPrinterTurbo
entries.what_it_does: A one-stop AI short-video generator: give it a topic or keyword and it writes the script with an LLM (many providers supported, including Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, Groq, OpenRouter and local Ollama), matches stock footage from Pexels/Pixabay/Coverr (or your own local media), generates voiceover (Microsoft Edge TTS built in — free, no API key; many other TTS providers optional), burns in subtitles (TTS timestamps or local Whisper), adds background music, and composites an HD short with FFmpeg/MoviePy in 9:16, 16:9 or 1:1. It can batch-generate, publish finished videos to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts, and is driven four ways: Streamlit WebUI, FastAPI REST API, CLI, and an agent skill file for coding agents. No GPU is required.
entries.fit_rationale: The closest off-the-shelf match in this wave to what VyralX's autopilot already does (topic → script → voice → stock footage → captioned short → publish), and its free path is real: Edge TTS + free stock APIs + a free-tier LLM. Two constraints stop a straight adopt: it requires Python 3.11+ while the fleet runs Python 3.10 (the fleet Python upgrade is already the known unblock for other held work), and a Streamlit + MoviePy/FFmpeg rendering stack is far beyond a ~180 MB service budget on the ~956 MB VMs — rendering belongs in batch on the owner's machine or post-upgrade capacity. Adapt its pipeline stages and provider fallbacks into VyralX rather than running a second full stack beside the existing autopilot.

entries.name: OpenCut
entries.what_it_does: "The open-source CapCut alternative" — a free, open-source timeline video editor for web, desktop and mobile, matching the GitHub card shown on the source carousel's cover slide ("A free and open source video editor for web, desktop, and mobile"). Editing and rendering happen locally in the browser (multi-track timeline, captions, effects, export with no account and no watermark); the classic version is what runs today at opencut.app. Important status caveat from the repo's own README: the project is being rewritten from the ground up (Rust core, plugin-first architecture, an Editor API, an MCP server for AI agents, and a headless mode for automation/batch rendering); outside contributions are paused during the rewrite, and the previous version lives on as opencut-app/opencut-classic, which the README calls "the one to reach for today".
entries.language: TypeScript (classic web app); the in-progress rewrite is built around a Rust core
entries.fit_rationale: A human-facing manual editor, not an automation component: today it offers VyralX no API, MCP or headless path (those are promised in the unfinished rewrite), and VyralX's pipeline is agent-driven rendering, not hand-editing. Its value now is as the owner's free manual finishing editor on his own machine when a VyralX video needs a human touch-up, replacing CapCut Pro without a subscription. Revisit for integration only when the rewrite's MCP server / headless mode actually ships.

entries.name: AgentTube — YouTube Automation Agent
entries.what_it_does: A self-hosted, open-source AI agent that runs a YouTube channel end to end under the name **AgentTube** (the branding used by the repo's current README text and every index of it; the repo itself is named youtube-automation-agent). It researches topics and builds a content strategy, writes scripts, generates narration and visuals, assembles real MP4s (free local slideshow rendering by default; paid AI-video providers optional and capped), writes titles/descriptions/tags, and — only after human approval — schedules and publishes, then learns from analytics, retention curves and comments, proposing changes the owner approves. Notable workflow pieces: an autonomous channel operator driven by a channel mandate, production-readiness checks, resumable checkpointed generation, a Scene Repair Studio (fix one scene without restarting), a Shorts Repurposing Studio, comment mining for video ideas, and controlled title/thumbnail growth experiments. Runs on Node.js 18.17+ with your own keys; Gemini's free tier covers text and narration; YouTube Data API v3 + Analytics API credentials are required.
entries.fit_rationale: Directly overlaps VyralX's existing, production-verified YouTube autopilot, so adopting a second full channel-running stack (Node + Playwright/Chromium rendering) makes no sense on the ~956 MB fleet. What is worth adapting is its workflow discipline, which is stronger than a plain uploader: approval-first publishing gates, resumable checkpointed production, scene-level repair, Shorts repurposing from approved long videos, and an analytics/comment learning loop where every lesson needs owner sign-off — all patterns that harden VyralX's autopilot without new infrastructure.

entries.name: ULTRON Orb UI (Sagar Tamang)
entries.what_it_does: **Only the orb user interface of the creator's ULTRON assistant — nothing more.** It is a Next.js + Three.js holographic orb (layered wireframe shells, a spiral inner core, floating code-text sprites, orbiting debris, dust particles, scan rings, bloom + chromatic-aberration post-processing) with a HUD, controlled by mouse/touch, keyboard, or bare-hand gestures through a webcam (MediaPipe HandLandmarker: one pinched hand spins the orb, two pinched hands zoom). It runs locally with `npm install && npm run dev`. **Caveat, in the creator's own words (his project write-up, mirrored in the repo README): "The voice agent and the device-control layer are proprietary for now" — the real-time voice conversation and the Android device control demoed in the reel are NOT in this repo and are not open source.** This card covers the orb UI only, and the fit below is judged on the UI alone.
entries.fit_rationale: Judged purely as a UI: a lightweight, client-side, MIT-licensed orb is a strong visual centrepiece for FRIDAY's website voice page — the "talk to the orb" surface the owner wants FRIDAY to feel like — and the gesture control is a bonus that costs nothing server-side (it runs in the visitor's browser, so the ~956 MB fleet is untouched). Adapt it by wiring the orb's animation state to FRIDAY's real voice session (idle / listening / thinking / speaking), which the repo does not do — it ships no voice integration at all, so nothing here substitutes for the LiveKit/Gemini voice work.

entries.name: SANA-WM (NVIDIA Sana world model)
entries.what_it_does: SANA-WM is NVIDIA's 2.6B-parameter open-source world model (released 2026/05, Stage-1 training released 2026/07): it turns one image plus a camera trajectory into 720p, minute-long, controllable video, with precise 6-DoF camera control via a dual-branch (coarse global pose + fine pixel-aligned) controller and hybrid linear attention (frame-wise Gated DeltaNet + periodic softmax) for long-horizon coherence. An optional second-stage 17B long-video refiner sharpens stage-1 output. The wider Sana repo is NVIDIA's efficiency-oriented training/inference codebase for the whole Sana family (image, SANA-Video, SANA-Streaming, Sol-RL).
entries.fit_rationale: Reject for the fleet on hardware alone, same reason as LTX-2: its own project page says inference needs a single H100 for a one-minute 720p clip (the distilled NVFP4 variant runs on a single RTX 5090, ~34s per 60s clip; training took 15 days on 64 H100s). FRIDAY's fleet has no GPU at all (two ~956MB-RAM VMs), and the free-only rule rules out paid hosted GPU generation as a default. Interesting as a world-model reference for VyralX's video roadmap only if GPU hardware ever arrives.

entries.name: Locally Uncensored
entries.what_it_does: A free, open-source all-in-one local AI studio desktop app (Windows and Linux, macOS/Android in beta): chat, image generation, video generation and a coding agent in one window, everything running on the user's own machine with no Docker, no terminal and no config files. It auto-detects or installs a local engine (Ollama / LM Studio / its own llama.cpp-based engine) and ComfyUI for media, ships a model manager that marks which models fit the user's hardware and downloads them in one click, and markets "uncensored" (non-refusing) models alongside mainstream ones in the same menu. Optional paid LU Labs Cloud exists for hosted larger models, but local mode is the product.
entries.fit_rationale: Learn from it, don't integrate: the useful ideas for FRIDAY are the UX patterns — zero-config install, a model manager that honestly marks what fits the hardware, and chat/create/code in one window — which map onto the owner's laptop/phone client ambitions. The app itself doesn't fit the fleet: it's a desktop local-model studio (media generation needs a real GPU the fleet and the owner's current setup don't provide for it), its AGPL-3.0 licence would encumber anything FRIDAY copied code from, and its "uncensored" positioning is not a FRIDAY requirement — FRIDAY is a server/voice-first assistant, not a local desktop studio.

entries.name: Free Claude Code (FCC)
entries.what_it_does: A local proxy that lets coding harnesses — Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, VS Code, Pi, OpenCode and 6 others (12 harnesses total) — run on free AI models instead of paid Anthropic/OpenAI endpoints, exposing Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Chat Completions, OpenAI Responses and Gemini API surfaces with native streaming/tool use preserved. Its README headline is exactly the reel's fingerprint: **61 supported providers** (free, paid, subscription and local) aggregating **1.3B+ free tokens per month**, with automatic retries, rate-limit/concurrency controls, model/provider fallback and multi-API-key fallback. The reel's "~58,000 stars" has since grown — the repo now shows ~70,640 stars. The project states it follows provider ToS and removes integrations if they stop being allowed, and is not affiliated with Anthropic.
entries.license: AGPL-3.0 per its README badge (GitHub classifies the licence as "Other")
entries.fit_rationale: Inference already implements this exact pattern in production (multi-provider free-tier key pool, failover, quota ledger, best-suitable routing — same verdict as FreeLLMAPI and OmniRoute, both already carded from this corpus). Do not duplicate it. The only cherry-picks are its provider catalogue breadth (61 providers worth diffing against Inference's pool) and its harness-side trick of preserving native streaming/tool use while swapping the model behind Claude Code-class clients, which is relevant to Forge's coding-agent work.

entries.name: Codex ↔ ChatGPT Web bridge (codex-chatgpt-web)
entries.what_it_does: A launcher that makes ChatGPT Web (including Pro) appear as a native model inside OpenAI's Codex, "without using Codex quota": messages run through the user's signed-in ChatGPT Web session in an embedded browser (Playwright-style automation), preserving context, streaming, images and — in "Full harness" mode — Codex's local files/terminal/tools via an MCP tunnel connector created in ChatGPT Developer Mode. Models offered depend on the ChatGPT account (Free/Go get smaller web models; paid accounts get the flagship web models). Its own README is candid: "This is unofficial browser automation, not an OpenAI API," the browser profile is a sensitive login artifact, and it is "not affiliated with or endorsed by OpenAI."
entries.fit_rationale: Reject on terms-of-service grounds: the tool's whole purpose is to spend a consumer ChatGPT subscription's web allowance programmatically through a coding agent, via automated browser control of a product OpenAI offers for interactive human use — not through any API or plan OpenAI sells for that use. That is borrowing a consumer allowance outside its intended channel, with real account-suspension risk for the account involved. FRIDAY's standing rule is legitimate free tiers and official APIs only, so Inference must not adopt this route (or its pattern) even though the engineering is competent. Use sanctioned free API tiers (Gemini/Groq/OpenRouter/NVIDIA NIM, already in Inference's pool) instead.

entries.name: Bytez (hosted model-inference service)
entries.what_it_does: One API key and one unified protocol for serverless inference over a very large catalogue of open-source models (text, image, video, audio across ~33 ML tasks), plus pass-through access to closed models (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google etc.), a model hub, an arXiv-grounded agent and a papers feed. No server/product code is published — like Uplika, this is a service entry, not a repo adoption.
entries.license: Not applicable — closed hosted service (docs repo carries no product licence)
entries.language: None — no product code (docs repo is TypeScript)
entries.fit_rationale: Candidate Inference provider route on the free tier only: a documented $0 tier exists, so it passes the owner's FREE-only rule as a trial — but a narrow one. Only ≤7B open models at 1 concurrent request are free, which suits just Inference's cheap/fast lane (classification, short rewrites), not its main reasoning traffic, and inference is credit-metered so any use beyond the $0 allowance would be paid spend and stays off. Action if pursued: create a free account, empirically confirm what free credit/token volume the $0 tier actually grants before counting it in the quota ledger, and wire it in as a low-priority pool member behind the existing Gemini/Groq/OpenRouter/NIM routes. If the trial shows the $0 tier grants no usable recurring volume, downgrade this card to reference-only.

entries.name: ULTRON (Ard!t — arditbe/UltronAI) — PRIORITY / owner's reference reel
entries.what_it_does: The repo named by the ULTRON creator himself (Ard!t, `arditbe`) in the comments of the owner's reference reel. Per its README (verbatim gist): "ULTRON: an AI that lives in your Mac. It hears you, watches through your webcam, takes over your apps and unlocks your screen. It follows you to your iPhone." It is a local-first, Node.js desktop assistant: you start it once and it keeps listening — voice in/out, webcam vision, screen reading, mouse/keyboard/app control, terminal commands, website building, persistent memory in a local `memory/` folder, and a self-built native iPhone app in `ios/` (paired over Tailscale, can place a real incoming-call screen). The brain is a LOCAL Ollama model — default `gemma3:12b` (~8 GB download, 16 GB RAM recommended; `gemma3:4b` on 8 GB, `gemma3:27b` on 32 GB+; an Ollama-cloud `gpt-oss:120b-cloud` option also exists). **What is public vs what the reel demos — precisely:** unlike the other ULTRON card in this corpus (Sagar Tamang's, where only the orb UI is public and the voice/device layer is explicitly proprietary), THIS repo's root listing does contain the claimed layers as source folders/files: `control/`, `tts/`, `term/`, `memory/`, `ios/`, plus `server.js`, `gemini.js`, `windows.js`, voice-setup scripts (`setup-voice.sh/.ps1/.bat`) and `set-unlock-password.sh`. So on paper the public repo covers the reel's two headline behaviours — continuous voice conversation and autonomous computer control. **Caveats that cap that claim:** the repo was created 2026-11-15 (one day before this check), has only 4 commits and 0 releases, no `.exe`/`.dmg` (runs from source), and none of it was executed or tested for this card — code presence is verified, working behaviour is not. Its own Safety section states it "runs commands without asking by default" (only dangerous ones ask), which is the opposite of FRIDAY's confirmation gates.
entries.license: None — no License field on the GitHub page and no LICENSE file in the root listing. That means all-rights-reserved by default: the code can be read, but not legally copied or adapted into FRIDAY.
entries.language: JavaScript (Node.js 20+; `server.js`/`gemini.js`/`package.json`, plus shell/PowerShell scripts and a Swift iPhone app under `ios/`)
entries.fit_rationale: This is the closest public artefact to the owner's ULTRON reference experience, so mine it as the design reference for the Laptop-Phone and voice lanes: always-listening local assistant, one companion that spans computer + phone (Tailscale pairing, phone-as-remote with an incoming-call surface), memory as plain local files, push-to-talk (Space) / stop (Esc). It cannot be adopted or adapted as code for three independent reasons: (1) NO LICENCE — reuse is not permitted; (2) fleet-infeasible — it needs a local 4B–27B Ollama model (8 GB download, 8–32 GB RAM) and Node 20 on a desktop with webcam/mic/accessibility permissions, against FRIDAY's 956 MB RAM servers, ~180 MB per-service caps, Python 3.10 and no GPU — it could only ever run on the owner's laptop, never on the fleet; (3) unproven and unsafe-by-default — 4 commits, zero releases, and an auto-authorize command model FRIDAY must not copy. FRIDAY's equivalent path stays its own: Gemini Live voice + LiveKit, Memora, and a gated laptop/phone executor — judged against this repo's *feel*, not its code.
entries.friday_agent_raw: Laptop-Phone-control / FRIDAY voice (reference architecture); Memora (local `memory/` folder pattern)

entries.name: ULTRON (AbuZar-Ansarii) — a different repo, NOT the creator's
entries.what_it_does: A Python desktop "autonomous desktop intelligence" with an MCU Ultron (James Spader) persona: voice-first control of a Windows/macOS/Linux workstation through 51 auto-discovered native tools, a PyQt6 holographic HUD, and Gemini Live as the session engine (config: a free Google Gemini API key; Ollama/OpenAI also listed as providers). Headline modules per the README: Project Prometheus (writes, compiles and hot-loads new Python tools at runtime), Chronos (background context/fatigue watchdog), Minority (OpenCV gesture control), Cerebro (local SQLite knowledge graph with TF-IDF vector RAG), Genesis (Home Assistant room lighting), Deep-Vocal (offline TTS with a DSP "Spader warp"), plus Ghost Pilot mouse/keyboard takeover, Face-ID sentry, network auditing, browser/Playwright control, an Android ADB/scrcpy bridge and sub-agent "drone swarms". **Provenance — read carefully:** this is a DIFFERENT project from the reference reel's ULTRON. It was linked by a commenter on the same reel (sweep crew-01 extracted.json records only the bare comment URL "https://github.com/AbuZar-Ansarii/Ultron" for DftRj2yKIoN); the reel's creator named `arditbe/UltronAI` instead (see arditbe-ultronai.md). Nothing on this repo's page connects it to the creator or the reel, and its capability claims ("6 God-Tier Superhuman Capabilities") are README assertions — none were tested for this card.
entries.license: MIT — stated in the README's License section and its license badge; note there is no LICENSE file in the root listing and no License field in the GitHub repository details, so the MIT claim rests on the README/badge alone
entries.fit_rationale: A pattern catalogue, not a component: the useful ideas for FRIDAY are mood/intent workspace presets (coding/gaming/research modes that set up apps, volume, lighting together), a local SQLite knowledge-graph memory with semantic recall (a Memora design input), and hot-loadable tool actions (a Forge design input). It cannot run in the fleet: it is a desktop GUI app (PyQt6 HUD, OpenCV, OS-level control) needing Python 3.11+ against the fleet's Python 3.10, a display, webcam/mic and a desktop OS — the 956 MB headless servers with ~180 MB per-service caps are the wrong machine entirely; at most it could run on the owner's laptop, where FRIDAY already has its own laptop-client direction. Treat the extravagant capability list as unverified marketing until independently tested.
entries.friday_agent_raw: Laptop-Phone-control / FRIDAY (desktop-assistant pattern); Memora (Cerebro graph pattern)

entries.name: ECC — Everything Claude Code (affaan-m)
entries.what_it_does: "The agent harness performance optimization system" for coding agents (formerly everything-claude-code). A single installable plugin (`ecc@ecc`) that gives Claude Code — and, with capability-limited adapters, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini, Zed, GitHub Copilot, Antigravity, Qwen and others — a fixed engineering process: plan → test → implement → review → verify → remember → improve. Counts on the GitHub page as checked: **71 agents, 314 skills and 98 legacy command shims**, plus hooks, rules, memory/continuous-learning ("instincts"), and AgentShield security scanning of prompts, hooks, MCP configs, permissions and secrets. (The source reel's "63 agents" framing is out of date against the live page's 71.) The OSS repo is free and MIT forever per the README; a separate hosted GitHub App ("ECC Pro", private repos from $19/seat/mo) exists and is NOT part of the free repo.
entries.language: TypeScript / JavaScript (Node.js 18+; README language badges also list Shell, Python, Go, Java, Perl and Markdown — most of the payload is skills/agents/rules content rather than a runtime)
entries.fit_rationale: Not a fleet component at all: ECC is a developer-harness plugin that runs wherever the coding agent runs (developer's machine), so the 956 MB servers, ~180 MB service caps and Python 3.10 are untouched — fleet feasibility is a non-issue precisely because nothing deploys to the fleet. The value to FRIDAY is process, mined selectively for Forge and for FRIDAY Universe's own multi-agent engineering workflow: specialised review/security/build-repair agents, skills-over-prompts packaging, hooks that enforce verification, and AgentShield-style scanning of agent configs and secrets. Adapt individual skills/agents rather than installing the whole 71-agent/314-skill surface (context bloat, and it is Claude-Code-shaped, not FRIDAY-shaped). Skip ECC Pro entirely under the owner's FREE-only rule — the MIT OSS core is the only part in scope.

entries.name: Helix (thalha-a9)
entries.what_it_does: An open-source username OSINT checker ("Decode the digital DNA of any identity"). It checks one username across roughly twelve thousand sites — the page title says 11,663 sites; the README body gives 11,956 sites as of 10 Nov 2026 (Sherlock + WhatsMyName + Maigret databases plus ~3,673 fediverse servers, each site checked once) — and re-checks every hit live against made-up "control probe" usernames, claiming 0 false positives on made-up names in sealed, re-runnable benchmark runs. Beyond existence it scores identity confidence (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW — a username match alone is never above LOW), matches avatars by perceptual hash, follows declared cross-platform links, and renders all of it as one standalone interactive D3.js graph HTML file. Extras: `--save-pages`/`--record-attempt` sealed evidence (hashed pages and run records), breach lookups behind an approved-subject gate, `--watch` change history, a `--me` self-audit mode, and a `--json` machine-readable output (`helix.cli.v1`). Install: `pipx install helix-osint`. Built for "security research, bug bounty reconnaissance, and OSINT education" per the README, with a Legal & Ethics section.
entries.language: Python (3.9+, aiohttp; badge on the page: Python 3.9+)
entries.fit_rationale: The strongest fleet fit in this batch: pure Python 3.9+ (fleet runs 3.10 ✓), MIT, free, no GPU, a CLI/library rather than a daemon, with a JSON mode designed for other programs to call. Adapt it as an on-demand IntelX tool, never a resident service: run bounded scans (single-database or capped site lists, concurrency kept low — the README itself warns high concurrency makes healthy sites time out) so a run stays inside the ~180 MB per-service envelope on the 956 MB servers, and keep the approved-subject gate — OSINT lookups only on subjects the owner names. Its control-probe verification discipline (re-check every hit against an impossible name before reporting) is also a transferable pattern for IntelX/Sentinel reporting generally. Caveat: at 45 stars and 29 commits it is young — pin a version and re-verify the false-positive claim on a known username before trusting output.

entries.name: OpenDirectory Finder (ewasion)
entries.what_it_does: A single static web page whose entire pitch on GitHub is "Just like filechef.com but it doesn't suck." The repo contains exactly two files — `index.html` and `README.md` (the README is a one-line title) — and is the source of the hosted page the source reel lists (ewasion.github.io/opendirectory-finder/): a form that builds search-engine queries for finding files (movies, music and other media, per the reel's framing of "searching hidden files like movies and music across the web") sitting in openly indexed web directories. There is no backend, no API, no tests and no documentation beyond the title.
entries.license: None — no License field on the GitHub page and no LICENSE file (root contains only `index.html` and `README.md`)
entries.fit_rationale: Nothing to take: (1) the functionality is a trivial search-query builder that IntelX already exceeds with ordinary web search — there is no code, data or technique here FRIDAY lacks; (2) no licence, so even the single page cannot be legally reused; (3) it has been untouched since 2017 (3 commits total); (4) its stated use — locating openly indexed copies of movies/music — is piracy-adjacent discovery, not a capability FRIDAY should build a lane around. Fleet feasibility is moot (a static page would cost nothing to host, which is the only sense in which it "fits" the 956 MB servers). Recorded for completeness of the sweep; do not implement.

entries.name: Escrcpy (viarotel-org)
entries.what_it_does: "Display and control your Android device graphically with scrcpy" — a free, open-source Electron GUI front-end for Genymobile's scrcpy (see scrcpy.md, already carded as **adopt** for the transport layer). Features per the README: an embedded mirror window that auto-fits resolution/orientation, keyboard mapping (touch, joystick, swipe, scroll, automation mappings drawn on the mirror), simultaneous multi-device control with broadcast input, batch screenshots and APK installs, a draggable control bar (rotation, screenshot, apps, files, terminal, AI assistant, automation), an MCP-based "Copilot" AI assistant for device control, visual automation scripts with image recognition, wireless ADB with LAN auto-discovery and Gnirehtet reverse tethering, and global hotkeys. Cross-platform desktop builds (Windows/macOS/Linux) via GitHub Releases and Homebrew. Note from the README: some advanced features come from a separate private extension repo (EscrcpyX) offered on a paid basis — the core GUI here is the free part.
entries.fit_rationale: Adopt the released desktop app as-is on the owner's laptop as the human-facing GUI over the already-adopted scrcpy transport for the Laptop-Phone lane (mirror + control the owner's realme phone, batch APK installs, wireless ADB) — that part costs the fleet nothing, since an Electron desktop app can never run on the 956 MB headless servers and was never meant to. Adapt, rather than merely adopt, at the automation layer: its MCP-based Copilot and visual automation scripts are the design reference for letting FRIDAY itself drive the phone through the same scrcpy/ADB channel, instead of a second, parallel control stack. Skip the paid EscrcpyX extension entirely under the owner's FREE-only rule — the Apache-2.0 core covers the mirror/control need.

entries.name: Robin
entries.what_it_does: An AI-powered tool for conducting dark web OSINT investigations. It leverages LLMs to refine an investigation query, filter search results from dark web search engines (searches run through Tor, which the tool requires), scrape the resulting pages, and provide an investigation summary. Features include multi-model support (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Mistral, OpenRouter, Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible API), a Streamlit web UI, MCP support (run Robin from any MCP-capable agent, using that agent's own model), grounded conversational follow-ups on a saved investigation, and one-click pivot queries; Docker deployment is the recommended install. Slug note: the source reel's narration was transcribed in the sweep as GitHub user "apursinghgautam" — the real user is **apurvsinghgautam** (Apurv Singh Gautam), whose GitHub profile states "Creator of Robin, an AI-powered dark web OSINT tool"; the repo is `apurvsinghgautam/robin`.
entries.fit_rationale: Adapt the investigation pattern into IntelX, do not deploy the tool as-is. The transferable design is concrete: LLM query refinement → Tor-routed search → scrape → LLM filtering/summary, exposed optionally as MCP, and especially its ingestion hygiene — scraped text is returned inside untrusted-data delimiters with control, zero-width and bidi characters stripped first, so the model reads it as evidence rather than instructions; that is a direct lesson for IntelX/Sentinel handling of untrusted web content. The runtime does not fit the fleet: a resident Streamlit UI plus a Tor daemon plus a scraping pipeline is not a ~180MB service on a ~956MB VM, a Tor investigation takes minutes, it needs an LLM API key, and running dark-web scraping from the production fleet's IPs is the wrong risk posture. Any use stays defensive-only (threat-intelligence research for Sentinel/IntelX, no interaction with dark-web services), on-demand and off the production VMs or post-ARM, within a scope the owner has approved.

entries.name: WanGP (formerly Wan2GP)
entries.what_it_does: A one-stop local "super app" for open-source generative models — create videos, images, music, speech and 3D assets, then step inside interactive worlds — billed as "The best Open Source Generative Models Accessible to the GPU Poor". Video models include Wan 2.1/2.2 and derived models, MiniMax H3, LTX-2/2.3/2.5, Hunyuan Video 1/1.5, LongCat, Kandinsky and LTXV; image models include Flux 1/2, Qwen Image, Krea 2 and Z-Image; plus many TTS/audio and 3D models. It provides a full web (Gradio) interface, LoRA support, many quantised checkpoint formats (int8, fp8, gguf, NV FP4, Nunchaku), a generation queue, headless batch mode, an API and an MCP interface, with architecture-aware model downloads for low-VRAM GPUs.
entries.license: Other (NOASSERTION on GitHub; a `LICENSE.txt` file is present in the repo — the README states WanGP is free to use locally and will never ask for a licence fee; the underlying models carry their own licences)
entries.fit_rationale: Reject for the fleet on the same hardware facts as LTX-2 (wave 1). "GPU Poor" still means a GPU: the README's own floor is running select models with as little as 4GB of VRAM (8GB of VRAM to get started with its interactive worlds), and its install paths target GTX 10XX / RTX 20XX–50XX cards with PyTorch/CUDA (the current path upgrades to Python 3.11 / PyTorch 2.10 / CUDA 13). The fleet has no GPU at all — two ~956MB-RAM VMs with ~180MB per-service caps and Python 3.10 — and the multi-GB model weights alone exceed a VM's RAM; the FREE-only rule rules out rented/hosted GPU generation as a default. Revisit only if the owner gets GPU hardware of his own: on a local GPU machine its low-VRAM optimisation, quantised checkpoints and all-in-one model coverage would make it a strong VyralX candidate, and it would subsume the LTX-2 route rejected earlier.

entries.name: DeepSeek Harness
entries.what_it_does: DeepSeek AI's open-source agent harness (`dsh`): the runtime scaffolding that turns a model into an agent, built on an "everything is a plugin" architecture powered by Cordis (described in the paper *A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability*) — model adapters, tools, the sandbox, session storage, the UI and the agent loop itself are all swappable plugins. It runs from npm with `npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web` (Web UI on `http://127.0.0.1:3080` by default) or from source with pnpm. Slug verified exactly as named in the source reels — the repo is real under `deepseek-ai`; no differently-named official repo was found or needed. It is explicitly a developer preview: the README warns "THERE WILL BE COMPATIBILITY-BREAKING CHANGES" and points readers to a safety notice before running it.
entries.fit_rationale: FRIDAY Universe already is a model-plus-harness system (10 agents, its own orchestration, memory and tool layers), so adopting DeepSeek Harness would mean replacing FRIDAY's harness rather than extending it. It also does not fit the fleet as a runtime: it is a local, Node.js/TypeScript coding-agent harness built and run with pnpm, not a Python 3.10 service that could live inside the ~180MB per-service caps on the ~956MB VMs, and it is developer-preview software whose own README promises compatibility-breaking changes. Its value is as a design reference for FRIDAY's and Forge's harness work — everything-is-a-plugin composability (including the agent loop itself), swappable model adapters, full session traceability, and plugin discoverability via the `dsh-plugin` topic — to mine when hardening FRIDAY's own harness, not to adopt.

entries.name: QATS Trader API (QuantityProject)
entries.what_it_does: Public documentation for the QATS Trader API — the REST API that lets a trader's own bot, script or TradingView strategy trade a QATS Prop account (QATS Prop is a prop-trading programme for crypto and TradFi USDT perpetuals, priced from Binance and Bybit market data). The documented surface covers market data, account/risk state, orders, executions, positions and command recovery, and the repo includes Python, JavaScript and cURL examples, an OpenAPI spec and a Postman collection. **This repository contains documentation only** — its README states explicitly: "This repository contains documentation only. Trading keys, backend code and customer records are not included." There is no underlying open-source code repo: the QuantityProject GitHub account's only public repository is this docs repo (a Vite/GitHub Pages site), and the trading system itself is proprietary and hosted at prop.qats.us. The docs describe a free API sandbox for registered, verified QATS traders (a virtual $100,000 account with separate `qats_sandbox_` keys; sandbox orders never reach an exchange), with every API order passing the same server-side risk checks as a manual order, writes taking an `Idempotency-Key`, and uncertain results confirmed by command ID instead of being resent.
entries.license: None listed (no licence in the GitHub repository details and no LICENSE file in the repo root)
entries.fit_rationale: There is nothing to run, integrate or adopt: this is a docs-only repo for a third-party prop firm, and using the actual API means opening a QATS Prop account — its evaluations are a paid product (the initial funded accounts then operate in a simulated environment), which is paid spend under the FREE-only rule and a new venue outside Stratex's demo-only programme on Binance demo and OANDA practice; no QATS account should be created without an explicit owner decision. The research value for Stratex is the API design, which is genuinely well-shaped and worth copying into Stratex's own venue layer: idempotency keys on every write, confirming an uncertain order result by command ID instead of resending it, server-side risk checks a bot cannot bypass, and a free sandbox with a virtual $100,000 account and keys kept separate from any real evaluation.

entries.name: ComfyUI
entries.what_it_does: "The most powerful and modular diffusion model GUI, api and backend with a graph/nodes interface" — a node-based AI creation engine for visual professionals: build image, video, 3D, audio and text workflows by wiring nodes (load model, encode prompt, sample, decode, save), save/load workflows as JSON, expose sophisticated workflows through App Mode, and integrate them into production pipelines via its local API endpoints. It natively supports a very broad model catalogue — image models including Stable Diffusion 1.5, SDXL, SD3.5, Flux.1/Flux.2, Qwen Image and Z-Image; video models including Wan 2.1/2.2, LTX-Video 2/2.3, HunyuanVideo 1.5 and CogVideoX; plus ACE-Step audio, Hunyuan3D and text models — with asynchronous queueing, partial graph re-execution, smart VRAM/RAM management, model offloading and quantised-model support, and partner nodes for closed models. It runs locally via a desktop app, a portable install or a manual install, or on the official paid Comfy Cloud.
entries.fit_rationale: Reject for the fleet on hardware, not on merit — this is the canonical node-based generation UI and the engine several other carded tools (e.g. WanGP) are compared against. Its own README floor is still a GPU machine: it "can run even the biggest open source models on as low as 4GB vram + 8GB ram", its install paths target NVIDIA / AMD / Intel / Apple Silicon GPUs with current PyTorch/CUDA or ROCm builds, and it steers users to Python 3.13 (3.14 works, 3.12 as a fallback) — the fleet has no GPU at all, two ~956MB-RAM VMs in total, and Python 3.10, and the multi-GB checkpoint files alone exceed a VM's RAM. The only no-local-GPU route, Comfy Cloud, is the project's official paid cloud version, which the FREE-only rule rules out as a default. Revisit only if the owner gets GPU hardware of his own: on a local GPU machine ComfyUI would be VyralX's strongest generation backend, and its portable workflow-JSON format is the pattern any future VyralX workflow layer should stay compatible with.

entries.name: Jarvis (vierisid/jarvis — @usejarvis/brain)
entries.what_it_does: A self-hostable "company workflow brain" — "Your company workflow brain. AI for judgment. Code for repetition." The brain (daemon) keeps memory, conversations and workflows running: describe a recurring job in chat or on a visual canvas and run it manually, on a schedule, or from event/webhook triggers, combining app integrations, branching, loops, AI steps and approvals; a SQLite-backed memory vault stores facts, relationships, preferences and goals across tasks. A separate desktop app (the sidecar) connects a user's computers to that one brain over an authenticated WebSocket, giving it browser and desktop control, terminal commands, file access, screenshots and clipboard, subject to per-device permissions; it can also chat from Telegram or Discord, talk or type via the dashboard or the floating Pebble interface with voice and wake-word support, and is governed by Authority rules with approval requests, an audit trail, and pause/stop controls. Self-hosted setups are LLM-agnostic — Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Ollama and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, configured through Settings with model routing. This repository contains the brain, dashboard, workflow runtime and desktop app.
entries.license: Other (NOASSERTION on GitHub; the README states Jarvis is source-available under the Jarvis Source Available License 2.0, based on RSALv2 — a `LICENSE` file is present in the repo; this is a source-available licence with permitted-use restrictions, not an OSI open-source licence)
entries.language: TypeScript (Bun brain and React dashboard, with SQLite persistence and a vendored Activepieces workflow engine running in a subprocess; the desktop sidecar is Go)
entries.fit_rationale: Carded as a self-host packaging reference for FRIDAY, not as a component to adopt: Jarvis is a whole competing brain (memory vault, goals, workflow engine, Authority approvals, multi-machine sidecars), so running it would duplicate FRIDAY rather than extend it, and its source-available licence bars simply taking the code. Its runtime also does not fit the fleet as-is — a Bun/TypeScript daemon plus a React dashboard plus a separate workflow-engine subprocess plus a Go sidecar, on two ~956MB-RAM Python-service VMs. What FRIDAY should learn from it is the packaging, which is genuinely well-shaped: a one-command self-host (`bun install -g @usejarvis/brain`, then `jarvis start`; an install script that clones the repo under `~/.jarvis/daemon` and links the `jarvis` command; and a single Docker run against `ghcr.io/vierisid/jarvis:latest` for amd64/arm64 with all state in one volume), a brain on a single default port (3142) that serves in setup mode on first run, JWT-only access since 0.9 with a CLI enrollment-token flow for each device (`jarvis enroll`), and a complete day-to-day CLI surface — `jarvis status`, `doctor`, `logs`, `restart`, `stop`, `autostart`, `update`, and `export`/`restore` of a full backup. Self-hosting itself is free with the user's own model keys (managed hosting is the paid product), so studying and borrowing these patterns costs nothing under the FREE-only rule.
